one_line: Binary smoke masks are annotator-threshold artifacts: models trained on them learn the annotator's opacity threshold, not smoke.
problem: Smoke has no physical binary boundary; every binary ground-truth mask implicitly encodes where one annotator decided the density became 'enough'. What supervised models actually learn from such labels is unknown.
core_hypothesis: A segmentation model trained on one annotator's smoke masks internalizes that annotator's implicit transmittance threshold as a global scalar, and most cross-annotator disagreement in model evaluation is explained by this single latent threshold rather than by shape or localization error.
falsifiable_prediction: If the same smoke images are independently masked by two annotators with different strictness, a model trained on annotator A will score poorly against annotator B, but fitting a single global threshold offset on the model's soft output (one parameter) will recover the majority of the score gap; for solid objects the same one-parameter fix recovers almost nothing.
why_important: If true, much of the reported cross-dataset 'domain gap' in smoke segmentation is a labeling-threshold gap, and the field is spending architecture effort on a calibration problem.
why_possibly_novel: Cross-annotator studies exist for medical and generic segmentation, but treating annotator strictness as a recoverable one-parameter latent variable of the trained model, and using recovery rate as the diagnostic, does not appear to be a standard analysis for volumetric media (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take one smoke video dataset, re-annotate a few hundred frames with two instructed strictness levels ('any visible haze' vs 'clearly opaque smoke'), train on one, evaluate on the other with and without a fitted global threshold on the soft logits, and compare gap recovery against a solid-object control class.
main_risk: Annotator differences may be spatially structured (e.g. different treatment of plume tails vs cores), in which case a single global threshold cannot summarize them and the clean one-parameter story collapses.
community_default_belief: Ground-truth masks are treated as noisy but unbiased samples of a true object extent; disagreement is 'label noise' to be averaged away.
why_that_may_be_wrong: For continuous media there is no true extent to be noisy around; the threshold choice is a free parameter of the annotation protocol, so disagreement is systematic bias, not zero-mean noise.
fastest_falsification: Dual-strictness re-annotation of ~200 frames plus one threshold-fitting script on an existing trained model; no new training needed for the first-pass test.

one_line: Transparent-object segmentation conflates occupancy ('where the glass is') with photometric effect ('where the glass changes the image'), and model errors concentrate where the two diverge.
problem: Glass datasets label physical object extent, but the image evidence only exists where the glass measurably modulates light (edges, speculars, distortions). The task definition silently mixes two different targets.
core_hypothesis: Segmentation errors on transparent objects are not spatially random: they concentrate in the 'occupied but photometrically silent' set (flat clean glass over flat background), and this set can be predicted in advance from a simple local background-modulation score without running the model.
falsifiable_prediction: A per-pixel photometric-effect magnitude (difference between the scene with and without the object, available in controlled captures) will predict per-pixel model error with substantially higher correlation than distance-to-boundary or object size, across architectures.
why_important: It reframes 'glass is hard' into a measurable identifiability statement, separates errors models can fix from errors no RGB model can fix, and implies evaluation should stratify by photometric effect.
why_possibly_novel: Error analyses for glass segmentation usually stratify by boundary distance or object category; stratifying by physically measured background-modulation magnitude via paired with/without-object captures seems uncommon (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Capture a small paired dataset (scene with and without each glass object on a fixed tripod), compute per-pixel modulation magnitude, run several public transparent-object models, and regress per-pixel error on modulation magnitude vs geometric covariates.
main_risk: Paired captures constrain scenes to static tabletop settings, so the conclusion might not extend to in-the-wild glass such as storefronts and vehicles.
community_default_belief: Transparent objects are hard mainly because of confusing reflections and lack of texture; better context modeling will solve it.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Part of the failure set may carry literally zero object photons in the mixed signal; no amount of context modeling changes the per-pixel identifiability there, and the reachable improvement ceiling is lower than assumed.
fastest_falsification: One weekend-scale tabletop capture with a tripod and a handful of glass objects, then correlation analysis on existing pretrained models.

one_line: Alpha matting, not binary segmentation, is the correct output space for smoke; binary training actively destroys usable density information.
problem: Nearly all smoke segmentation pipelines binarize at the label level, before training. Whether this discards information the network otherwise represents is untested.
core_hypothesis: Networks trained with binary smoke masks still compute an internal soft-density estimate in intermediate features, and the binarizing head is where the information is lost; a matting-style head on the same backbone recovers density ordering without any density supervision.
falsifiable_prediction: A linear probe on penultimate features of a binary-trained smoke segmenter will rank-correlate with true transmittance (measurable on rendered or fog-machine data) far above chance, and swapping only the head to a soft target will improve downstream tasks that need density (visibility estimation) without hurting mask accuracy.
why_important: If density is already latent in binary-trained models, the community can upgrade existing systems by retraining heads only, and dataset builders should stop shipping binary-only labels.
why_possibly_novel: Linear-probing for a physically meaningful continuous quantity (transmittance) inside binary-trained media segmenters, as opposed to probing for classes or depth, appears little explored (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Render smoke with known per-pixel transmittance over varied backgrounds, train a standard segmenter on binarized labels only, then linear-probe features against the withheld transmittance; report rank correlation vs a randomly initialized backbone control.
main_risk: Synthetic-to-real gap: probes may exploit rendering artifacts, so a fog-machine validation set with measured optical depth is needed to confirm.
community_default_belief: Binary masks are an adequate target and soft matting is a niche refinement for compositing applications.
why_that_may_be_wrong: For media, the binary target is a lossy quantization of the only physically real quantity (optical depth); treating quantization as the task may cap performance and explain boundary instability.
fastest_falsification: Probe an existing public smoke model on rendered transmittance data; a null result (no decodable density) kills the strong version immediately.

one_line: Visible flame boundaries are exposure artifacts: the same fire produces different 'ground truth' masks depending on camera exposure, making fire GT a function of the sensor, not the scene.
problem: Fire is a volumetric light emitter with intensity spanning several orders of magnitude; where the 'flame' visibly ends depends on exposure time, gain, and tone mapping. Datasets ignore this.
core_hypothesis: The area of the human-annotated flame mask for a fixed physical fire varies systematically and substantially with exposure settings, and models trained on mixed-exposure data learn an average that is wrong for every specific exposure.
falsifiable_prediction: Bracketed-exposure captures of the same fires will yield annotator masks whose area grows monotonically with exposure; a model's error on a given image will correlate with the mismatch between that image's exposure and the training-set exposure statistics.
why_important: It implies fire segmentation benchmarks are not measuring a property of fire, and that exposure metadata (or HDR input) is a first-order requirement, not a nuisance factor.
why_possibly_novel: Camera-parameter-dependence of labels is discussed for low-light detection, but treating flame extent as intrinsically exposure-defined, with a quantitative mask-area vs exposure law, seems unexamined for segmentation (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Film several controlled fires with exposure bracketing, have annotators mask each bracket independently (shuffled, no side-by-side), and fit mask area as a function of exposure value; then stratify an off-the-shelf model's errors by exposure mismatch.
main_risk: Annotators may anchor on flame texture rather than brightness, making masks more exposure-stable than hypothesized; that itself would be an informative negative result.
community_default_belief: Flame extent is an objective scene property that annotators estimate with noise.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The luminous boundary of an emitter has no canonical threshold; the camera's response curve chooses it, so the 'object' is co-defined by the sensor pipeline.
fastest_falsification: One evening of bracketed captures of a fire pit plus independent annotation of ~50 frames.

one_line: 2D smoke masks are geometrically inconsistent across simultaneous viewpoints, proving the 2D task is a projection of an ill-posed problem models silently resolve with view-specific heuristics.
problem: A volumetric plume has no view-consistent silhouette at a fixed opacity threshold under different backgrounds and lighting per view; nobody has quantified how inconsistent the 2D labels are.
core_hypothesis: Multi-view captures of the same plume, annotated independently per view, will produce masks that cannot be explained by any single 3D density threshold; the inconsistency magnitude grows with plume thinness and background contrast difference between views.
falsifiable_prediction: Optimizing a 3D density field to jointly explain all per-view masks will leave a large irreducible residual for thin smoke (unlike for solid objects, where visual hulls are consistent), and the residual will correlate with per-view background luminance mismatch.
why_important: Quantifies exactly how much of the smoke segmentation task is not a property of the smoke, giving a principled noise floor for single-view methods and a case for density-field targets.
why_possibly_novel: Visual-hull consistency is a classical tool for solid shapes; using its failure as a measurement instrument for label ill-posedness of participating media appears rare (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Two or three synchronized cameras around a fog machine outdoors, independent annotation per view, then fit a voxel density grid with a shared threshold to all masks and measure per-view residual vs a solid-object control (e.g. a mannequin).
main_risk: Calibration and synchronization errors could masquerade as label inconsistency; the solid-object control is essential to bound rig error.
community_default_belief: Per-view 2D masks are consistent projections of one underlying object, so single-view learning is well-posed.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Perceived smoke extent depends on background radiance behind each ray, which differs per view; the 'object' literally has different shapes from different directions.
fastest_falsification: A two-camera fog-machine capture and a voxel fit; large residuals on smoke but not on the mannequin control settles the direction quickly.

one_line: Smoke ground truth in video is shutter-speed-dependent: motion blur redefines the plume boundary, so frame-level labels encode camera temporal sampling, not the medium.
problem: Turbulent smoke moves fast relative to typical shutter times; the imaged plume is a time-integral. Labels made on such frames inherit an integration window nobody records.
core_hypothesis: For the same physical plume, masks annotated on short-exposure frames are systematically smaller and more filamentary than masks on long-exposure frames, and models trained on one shutter regime degrade on the other in a directionally predictable way (over- or under-segmentation, not random error).
falsifiable_prediction: Dual-camera captures (fast and slow shutter, co-located) will show a consistent mask-area and boundary-complexity gap after annotation; cross-shutter model evaluation will show signed area bias matching the training regime.
why_important: Surveillance, drone, and phone cameras span wide shutter ranges; if the effect is real, deployment error has a knowable signed component correctable from EXIF-level metadata.
why_possibly_novel: Motion blur is studied as degradation for solid-object tasks; treating shutter time as part of the label definition for media, with signed-bias predictions, seems new as a framing (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Beam-split or side-by-side dual-shutter capture of fog-machine plumes, independent annotation, area/complexity statistics; then train small models per regime and measure signed cross-regime bias.
main_risk: Wind and turbulence variability may swamp the shutter effect unless captures are tightly paired in time.
community_default_belief: A video frame is a faithful snapshot of the scene; camera temporal parameters are irrelevant to what the object is.
why_that_may_be_wrong: For fast-mixing media the frame is a temporal average whose support genuinely depends on integration time; there is no shutter-independent 2D object to label.
fastest_falsification: Annotate paired fast/slow-shutter frames from one capture session and test the mask-area gap statistically.

one_line: Per-pixel classification is a category error for mixed pixels: cross-entropy training on media provably biases boundaries toward hard edges, and the bias is measurable as gradient sharpening.
problem: At smoke boundaries most pixels are physical mixtures (partial coverage / partial opacity). Classification losses force a decision on pixels that are genuinely fractional.
core_hypothesis: Cross-entropy-trained media segmenters exhibit output transition widths (logit gradient at boundaries) that are systematically narrower than the true alpha transition width, and this sharpening bias grows with training time; regression to alpha removes it.
falsifiable_prediction: On rendered smoke with known alpha profiles, the fitted sigmoid width of model outputs across boundaries will be significantly narrower than the true alpha profile width for CE-trained models, will shrink over training epochs, and will match truth for L1-on-alpha-trained models of identical architecture.
why_important: Identifies a specific, loss-induced, quantifiable distortion in every CE-trained media model, separating loss pathology from data or architecture issues.
why_possibly_novel: Boundary sharpening is folklore; a controlled measurement isolating the loss function as the cause on media with known alpha profiles, including training-time dynamics, appears not to be standard (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Single synthetic dataset with analytic alpha ramps of varied widths; train identical networks with CE vs alpha regression; fit transition widths at matched checkpoints.
main_risk: The effect might be dominated by label binarization rather than the loss itself; needs a condition with soft labels + CE to disentangle.
community_default_belief: Cross-entropy with binarized labels is a harmless default; boundary softness can be recovered by reading the logits as confidence.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Logits of a classifier estimate label probability, not mixing fraction; under annotator thresholding these diverge exactly at the boundary band, the only place softness matters.
fastest_falsification: One synthetic training run pair (CE vs regression) and a curve fit; a day of compute at small scale.

one_line: Transparent objects should be segmented by detecting background distortion, not object appearance: an explicit background-reconstruction branch is the load-bearing component.
problem: Glass has almost no appearance of its own; its image evidence is a structured error between the observed image and the plausible unoccluded background. Current models entangle this inference implicitly.
core_hypothesis: The information a network uses to find glass is predominantly 'this region disagrees with the expected background continuation'; making that explicit (predict the background, segment where reconstruction residual is structured) generalizes to unseen glass shapes and categories better than direct mask prediction at equal capacity.
falsifiable_prediction: On a shape-held-out split (train on containers, test on flat panes and irregular glass art), a reconstruct-then-compare model will lose less performance relative to its in-distribution score than a direct-mask model; ablating the reconstruction branch will collapse the gap.
why_important: If the mechanism is background-anomaly detection, then glass segmentation inherits all the machinery and theory of anomaly detection, and category-balanced datasets stop being necessary.
why_possibly_novel: Reconstruction-based anomaly detection is standard in industrial inspection; positioning it as the primary mechanism (with a shape-transfer test as the discriminating evidence) for transparent object segmentation is a specific untested claim (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build both models on the same backbone and data; define shape-held-out splits from existing transparent-object data by shape clustering; compare relative generalization drops.
main_risk: Inpainting-quality confound: a weak background model could sink the approach for reasons unrelated to the hypothesis; needs an oracle-background upper-bound condition using paired captures.
community_default_belief: Glass segmentation improves through better boundary modules and reflection-aware attention over the object region itself.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The object region carries almost no invariant appearance; boundary and reflection cues are sparse special cases of the general background-modulation signal, so modeling the background is the more complete route.
fastest_falsification: Oracle test first: with paired with/without-object captures, check whether thresholding structured residuals alone already localizes glass; if not, the mechanism claim dies cheaply.

one_line: Smoke, fire, fog, and dust need a third annotation ontology category ('media') distinct from stuff and things, and annotator agreement will jump when it exists.
problem: Panoptic ontologies force annotators to treat a plume either as a countable thing or as amorphous stuff; both choices create inconsistent instance boundaries and disagreement that is blamed on annotator quality.
core_hypothesis: A large share of inter-annotator disagreement on smoke/fire in panoptic-style annotation is caused by the ontology (thing-vs-stuff forced choice), not by perceptual difficulty, and introducing an explicit 'media' category with its own rules (no instance identity, soft extent allowed) measurably increases agreement at fixed annotation time.
falsifiable_prediction: In a controlled annotation study with the same images and annotators under two protocols (standard panoptic vs media-augmented), inter-annotator IoU/consistency on smoke and fire regions will be significantly higher under the media protocol, while solid-object agreement is unchanged.
why_important: Ontology is upstream of every dataset; if the category system is the bottleneck, no downstream modeling fixes it, and dataset builders have a cheap intervention.
why_possibly_novel: The stuff/things dichotomy has been criticized in general, but a controlled A/B annotation experiment isolating ontology-induced disagreement specifically for volumetric media appears missing (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Recruit a small annotator pool, annotate a shared image set under both protocols in counterbalanced order, and compare agreement statistics per category.
main_risk: Agreement gains might come trivially from the media protocol permitting vaguer labels, so the study must also measure downstream utility (e.g. training on each label set and testing on physically defined ground truth).
community_default_belief: Thing/stuff covers the visual world; smoke is just difficult stuff and disagreement reflects genuine ambiguity.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Part of the disagreement may be protocol-induced decision noise (where to cut instances, whether wisps count) that a fit-for-purpose ontology eliminates without touching perceptual ambiguity.
fastest_falsification: A two-protocol annotation pilot on ~100 images with 5 annotators.

one_line: Smoke boundaries are near-fractal, so boundary-based metrics do not converge as resolution increases; every boundary F-score for smoke is resolution-relative.
problem: Boundary metrics assume a rectifiable curve whose length stabilizes with finer sampling. Turbulent interfaces are famously multi-scale; whether annotation masks of smoke behave like rectifiable curves is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: The measured boundary length of high-effort smoke masks grows as a power law with image resolution (box-counting dimension noticeably above 1) over the practical resolution range, whereas solid-object masks plateau; consequently boundary-tolerance metrics change model rankings when evaluation resolution changes.
falsifiable_prediction: Computing box-counting dimension on finely annotated smoke masks will yield dimensions clearly above those of solid-object masks; re-evaluating a fixed pool of models at multiple resolutions will produce rank inversions on smoke but stable ranks on solids.
why_important: If rankings are resolution artifacts, published comparisons between smoke methods evaluated at different scales are not comparable, and metric design needs a scale-swept or scale-explicit definition.
why_possibly_novel: Fractal characterization of turbulent interfaces is classical fluid dynamics; importing it as a critique of segmentation boundary metrics with a rank-stability experiment appears novel in framing (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Commission a small set of very high resolution, high-effort smoke annotations; compute dimension estimates; evaluate several public models at 3-4 resolutions with standard boundary metrics and track rank correlation.
main_risk: Annotation effort limits: human masks may low-pass the true interface, understating the dimension and the effect; results should be reported as lower bounds.
community_default_belief: Boundary F-measures are a fair, resolution-agnostic way to compare fine-grained mask quality.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The tolerance radius interacts with a non-converging boundary length for fractal interfaces, so the metric measures a scale-dependent mixture of geometry and model quality.
fastest_falsification: Dimension estimate on a handful of maximal-effort masks; if smoke masks plateau like solids, the hypothesis dies before any model evaluation.

one_line: Inter-annotator disagreement maps on smoke are a free density sensor: disagreement rate is a monotone function of optical thickness.
problem: Disagreement between annotators on media is discarded or averaged, though it plausibly encodes the underlying continuous quantity that binary labels destroy.
core_hypothesis: Pixelwise annotator disagreement probability on smoke is a monotone (roughly sigmoidal) function of true transmittance, so a model trained to predict the disagreement map recovers relative optical depth ordering without any density supervision.
falsifiable_prediction: On scenes where transmittance can be measured (fog machine with calibrated backgrounds, or rendered smoke), multi-annotator disagreement frequency will rank-correlate strongly with transmittance in the mid-opacity band; a disagreement-trained model's output will inherit that correlation on held-out scenes.
why_important: Turns an artifact every multi-annotator dataset already contains into physical supervision, enabling density-aware smoke models with zero extra sensing.
why_possibly_novel: Using disagreement as an uncertainty proxy is known; validating it as a calibrated proxy for a specific physical variable (optical depth) and then training on it appears untested for media (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect 5-10 annotations per frame on fog-machine footage with checkerboard backgrounds (giving measurable contrast reduction), fit disagreement vs measured transmittance, then train a predictor of disagreement and evaluate its transmittance rank correlation on held-out footage.
main_risk: Disagreement also spikes at motion-blurred or cluttered regions regardless of density, potentially destroying monotonicity outside controlled scenes.
community_default_belief: Annotator disagreement is noise to be reduced via consensus and better guidelines.
why_that_may_be_wrong: For thresholded continuous quantities, disagreement is mathematically expected to peak where the quantity crosses the threshold spread, making it a measurement, not noise.
fastest_falsification: The disagreement-vs-transmittance curve fit on a single controlled capture session; non-monotonicity kills it.

one_line: Video-annotated smoke labels contain motion information that single-frame models cannot access, creating a hidden irreducible error floor in frame-level benchmarks.
problem: Annotators labeling video scrub frames and use motion to decide what is smoke, but many benchmarks and models consume single frames. The label channel and the input channel are mismatched.
core_hypothesis: A quantifiable fraction of smoke pixels in video-annotated datasets are statically ambiguous (indistinguishable from haze/walls/clouds in the single frame) and were resolved by the annotator using motion; single-frame model errors concentrate on exactly this subset, forming a floor no single-frame architecture can cross.
falsifiable_prediction: Re-annotating a sample of frames with annotators shown only the single frame (no scrubbing) will flip or blank a measurable subset of pixels; single-frame model errors will overlap this subset far above chance, and video models will beat single-frame models mostly on this subset and barely elsewhere.
why_important: Explains part of the persistent gap between video and image smoke methods as a supervision-information mismatch rather than architectural superiority, and gives benchmarks a principled 'static-resolvable' pixel partition.
why_possibly_novel: Input-label information asymmetry is discussed for temporal action tasks; a pixelwise partition of media datasets into motion-resolved vs static-resolved labels seems not to exist (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Single-frame re-annotation of a few hundred frames from a video-annotated smoke dataset, define the motion-resolved pixel set, stratify existing image-model and video-model errors over it.
main_risk: Single-frame annotators may guess from context, blurring the partition; needs a 'confident/unsure' response option to keep the set clean.
community_default_belief: Video models beat image models on smoke because temporal modeling is better feature engineering.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The advantage may be mostly that video models see the same channel the labels were made from; on statically resolvable pixels the architectures may tie.
fastest_falsification: The re-annotation study alone (no training) already tests whether a meaningful motion-resolved subset exists.

one_line: Annotation-tool signatures leak into smoke models: polygon vs brush tools imprint distinct boundary statistics that models learn and reproduce.
problem: Media boundaries are drawn with tools (polygons, brushes, smart-select) whose geometric priors differ enormously on diffuse boundaries, but tool provenance is not recorded or controlled.
core_hypothesis: Trained smoke segmenters reproduce the boundary-curvature and vertex-spacing statistics of the annotation tool used for their training data, and a classifier can identify the training-set tool from model outputs alone at high accuracy.
falsifiable_prediction: Annotating the same footage with polygon-only and brush-only protocols, then training matched models, will yield models whose output boundaries are separable by a simple statistical test (curvature spectrum, corner density); cross-tool evaluation will show a boundary-metric penalty absent in region metrics.
why_important: Reveals a concrete, correctable channel through which datasets teach geometry that has nothing to do with smoke, contaminating boundary-quality comparisons between methods trained on different datasets.
why_possibly_novel: Tool-induced label bias is anecdotal folklore; a controlled tool-A/B with model-output forensics for media boundaries appears undone (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Dual-tool annotation of one video set, matched training runs, boundary statistics comparison, and a train/test tool-identification probe on output masks.
main_risk: Annotator identity may confound tool identity unless annotators are crossed over both tools in the design.
community_default_belief: Annotation tools are interchangeable means to express the same ground truth; only annotator skill matters.
why_that_may_be_wrong: On boundary-undefined objects the tool's geometric prior fills the definitional vacuum, so the tool partially becomes the ground truth.
fastest_falsification: Compare curvature statistics of existing datasets known informally to use different tools; a null there weakens the claim before running the controlled study.

one_line: Trimap-style 'certain core + uncertain halo' smoke annotation dominates precise-boundary annotation in information per annotator-minute.
problem: Annotation budgets for smoke are spent tracing boundaries that are not physically real; the cost-information tradeoff of coarser but honest label geometries is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: For fixed annotation time, labeling smoke as (confident-smoke core, confident-background, unlabeled halo) yields models at least as good as precise-boundary labels on region metrics, and better calibrated in the halo band, because the halo honestly encodes ambiguity instead of a fabricated boundary.
falsifiable_prediction: In a time-controlled annotation study producing both label types over the same images, models trained on trimap labels (with the halo excluded from loss or treated as soft) will match full-mask models on core-region metrics and produce lower calibration error in the halo band.
why_important: Could cut media annotation cost substantially while improving uncertainty quality, directly changing how new smoke datasets get built.
why_possibly_novel: Trimaps are standard in matting; a time-controlled comparison against full masks as a training-label format for media segmentation, evaluated on calibration in the ambiguous band, appears missing (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Time-boxed dual-protocol annotation on one dataset, matched training, evaluation split into core/halo bands with region and calibration metrics.
main_risk: Halo exclusion shrinks effective supervised area; on small datasets the full-mask model might win simply via more supervised pixels.
community_default_belief: More precise boundaries are always better labels; coarse annotation is a compromise forced by budget.
why_that_may_be_wrong: When the boundary is fictional, precision spends budget encoding annotator whim; honest coarseness may carry strictly more usable information per minute.
fastest_falsification: Pilot with two annotators, 100 images, both protocols, small-model training; a large core-metric loss for trimaps ends it.

one_line: Smoke masks are systematically truncated in the downwind/diffusion direction, and models inherit a directional under-segmentation bias aligned with flow.
problem: Annotators stop labeling where they lose confidence, which for plumes is the diffuse downstream end; this produces a spatially anisotropic label bias no one measures.
core_hypothesis: The signed boundary error of human smoke masks (vs physically defined extent in controlled scenes) is largest and negative at the downstream end of plumes, and trained models reproduce this anisotropy: their misses concentrate downwind even on symmetric test plumes.
falsifiable_prediction: In fog-machine scenes with known emission and airflow direction, annotator masks will terminate at systematically higher density thresholds downstream than upstream; model predictions will show miss-rate as a function of angle-to-flow peaking downstream, in both matched and rotated/flipped test conditions.
why_important: Early-warning applications care most about the growing, diffuse frontier of a plume, exactly where this bias predicts silent failure.
why_possibly_novel: Directional annotation bias tied to a physical transport direction, and its inheritance by models, appears to be an unmeasured phenomenon (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Controlled plume captures with anemometer-logged flow direction, multi-annotator masking, signed-error-vs-direction analysis, then the same analysis on model outputs from public checkpoints.
main_risk: Flow direction correlates with density gradient by physics, so the analysis must dissociate 'bias beyond density explanation' via matched-density comparisons up/downstream.
community_default_belief: Annotation error on smoke is isotropic imprecision concentrated at boundaries generally.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Confidence-driven stopping is directional wherever the medium has a transport direction; error inherits the physics of dispersion.
fastest_falsification: Signed-error-vs-angle plot on one controlled capture with 5 annotators.

one_line: Majority-vote consensus masks are worse training targets than single-annotator masks for media, because vote-averaging fabricates a boundary no physical threshold produces.
problem: Consensus is the default for 'improving' labels, but on thresholded continuous fields the pixelwise majority of different-threshold annotators is not itself any consistent threshold of the field.
core_hypothesis: Models trained on per-annotator masks (randomly sampling one annotator per image, preserving internal consistency) outperform models trained on majority-vote masks of the same annotation pool, on both physically defined test labels and per-annotator test labels.
falsifiable_prediction: With a fixed multi-annotator pool, the sample-one-annotator training scheme will beat majority-vote training on smoke; on a solid-object control class the two schemes will tie or reverse, localizing the effect to boundary-undefined objects.
why_important: Directly contradicts a default dataset-construction practice; if true, existing multi-annotator media data should be re-released with per-annotator labels rather than consensus only.
why_possibly_novel: Label-aggregation critiques exist in classification; for segmentation of thresholded continuous media, the geometric inconsistency argument and the sample-vs-vote training comparison appear unexplored (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Use any multi-annotator smoke/fog annotation set (or create one, 5 annotators x few hundred frames); train matched models under vote vs sample schemes; evaluate against controlled-scene physical labels.
main_risk: Consensus reduces gross errors (mislabeled regions), which may outweigh boundary consistency; results may depend on annotator pool quality.
community_default_belief: Consensus labels are strictly cleaner and give better models than any individual annotator's labels.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Pixelwise voting destroys the within-annotator coherence (a consistent latent threshold) that models can otherwise absorb and calibrate away; the vote is cleaner pixelwise but incoherent object-wise.
fastest_falsification: Simulation first: threshold a known continuous field with simulated annotator thresholds, compare vote vs sample training on synthetic data in a day.

one_line: Self-overlapping transparency (glass behind glass) is where transparent-object labels and models both fail, because the label space cannot count layers.
problem: Binary glass masks cannot represent 'two layers here'; annotator behavior and model behavior on overlapping transparent surfaces are both undefined and unstudied.
core_hypothesis: Annotator disagreement and model error on transparent objects both spike specifically in multi-layer regions (a glass seen through another glass), and adding a per-pixel integer layer-count label resolves the annotation instability and improves single-layer mask accuracy as a side effect.
falsifiable_prediction: Constructed scenes with 0/1/2/3 glass layers will show annotator disagreement increasing steeply with layer count under binary protocols but staying flat under a layer-count protocol; models fine-tuned with an auxiliary layer-count head will improve on multi-layer regions without extra single-layer data.
why_important: Shelves, windows, vehicles, and laboratory scenes are full of stacked transparency; a label-space fix is cheaper than data scaling if the failure is representational.
why_possibly_novel: Layered depth and amodal ideas exist for opaque occlusion; per-pixel transparent-surface counting as an annotation and output space appears largely unexplored (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Tabletop scenes with controlled glass stacking, dual-protocol annotation, disagreement analysis, plus a small fine-tuning run with a counting head.
main_risk: Human ability to count transparent layers may itself cap out at two, limiting label quality for deeper stacks.
community_default_belief: Glass segmentation failures come from reflections and missing texture; overlap is just a harder instance of the same problem.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Overlap is a different problem class: the output space, not the feature space, lacks the expressiveness, so no amount of feature improvement fixes it.
fastest_falsification: Error and disagreement stratification by layer count on a small constructed set using existing public models and a few annotators.

one_line: Positives-only smoke annotation ignores 'proof of absence' evidence (crisp background visibility), inducing an over-segmentation bias in clutter that negative-evidence labels would fix.
problem: Annotators mark where smoke is, never where the scene's sharpness proves smoke is absent; the resulting supervision is asymmetric in a way that shapes model errors.
core_hypothesis: Because unmarked regions mix 'no smoke' with 'unsure', models treat low-texture unmarked regions as weakly positive, producing false positives on clean but hazy-looking areas; adding sparse explicit negative-evidence annotations (regions certified smoke-free by visible sharp detail) reduces false positives more per label than adding equal-cost positive labels.
falsifiable_prediction: Fine-tuning with a small budget of certified-negative region labels will cut false-positive rate on distractor scenes (fog-free haze-like surfaces, white walls, dust-free glare) substantially more than the same budget spent on additional positive masks.
why_important: False alarms dominate the practical cost of deployed smoke detection; a labeling-protocol change is far cheaper than model or data scale-ups.
why_possibly_novel: Negative/complementary labels exist in weak supervision literature; framing physically certified absence (sharpness as proof of no participating medium) as an annotation primitive for media seems specific and untested (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take a trained smoke model with a known false-positive profile; spend a fixed annotation budget two ways (more positives vs certified negatives) and compare false-positive reduction at matched true-positive rate.
main_risk: Certified negatives are easiest to find far from ambiguity, so naive collection may place them where models were never wrong; needs an active selection scheme, which complicates attribution.
community_default_belief: More positive annotations of the target class are the natural way to improve a segmenter; background is free supervision already.
why_that_may_be_wrong: For translucent media, the background class silently absorbs ambiguous pixels, so the 'free' negative supervision is contaminated exactly where it matters.
fastest_falsification: Budget-matched fine-tuning comparison on one model and one distractor-rich evaluation set.

one_line: Single-image smoke decomposition via a two-parameter Beer-Lambert model per pixel is identifiable under a low-frequency background prior, giving physics-grounded pseudo-labels for free.
problem: Smoke pixels follow I = t*B + (1-t)*A (transmittance t, background B, airlight-like smoke radiance A), but segmentation pipelines ignore this structure and learn appearance statistically.
core_hypothesis: Under a locally low-frequency background assumption, per-pixel transmittance is approximately identifiable from a single frame for mid-density smoke, and a solver based on this yields transmittance maps accurate enough to supervise a network that then beats mask-trained baselines on density-sensitive tasks.
falsifiable_prediction: On rendered smoke with known t, the closed-form/optimization decomposition will recover t with useful rank accuracy in the mid-density band and fail predictably in dense (t near 0) and thin (t near 1) bands; a network distilled from these pseudo-labels will inherit mid-band accuracy on real controlled captures.
why_important: Physics-grounded pseudo-labels sidestep the annotation-threshold problem entirely for the density band where most operational decisions happen.
why_possibly_novel: Dehazing uses closely related models globally; per-pixel local identifiability analysis for plume-scale smoke and its use as a segmentation supervision source appears under-explored (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement the decomposition, characterize its error vs true t on rendered data across background frequency content, then distill and test on fog-machine captures with measured contrast targets.
main_risk: Real backgrounds violate the low-frequency prior at edges and texture, potentially confining validity to too small a region set to supervise well.
community_default_belief: Physical image-formation models are too fragile for in-the-wild media; learned appearance is the practical route.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The claim has never been tested with the right target: not full-scene dehazing quality, but rank-accurate transmittance in the band where masks are ambiguous, which is a much weaker requirement.
fastest_falsification: The rendered-data identifiability study alone: if mid-band rank recovery fails even there, the idea is dead.

one_line: There is a computable per-pixel detectability limit for thin smoke (contrast vs noise), and model errors saturate this limit rather than reflecting model quality.
problem: Benchmarks penalize misses on thin smoke without asking whether the pixels carry any signal above sensor noise; model comparisons may be measuring noise-floor luck.
core_hypothesis: A physics-derived detectability index (local smoke-induced contrast change divided by local noise estimate) predicts per-pixel miss probability nearly deterministically across different architectures, implying current models are already at the information limit for thin smoke and remaining differences are elsewhere.
falsifiable_prediction: Across several public smoke models, per-pixel miss rate curves plotted against the detectability index will collapse onto approximately one curve; architectural differences will show up only above a detectability threshold, and reported cross-model gaps will shrink drastically when evaluation is restricted to detectable pixels.
why_important: Separates 'model is bad' from 'pixel is impossible', enabling honest benchmarks and redirecting effort from thin-smoke pixel chasing to detectable-band improvements or better sensing.
why_possibly_novel: Ideal-observer analyses are common in psychophysics and medical imaging; applying one as a benchmark-normalization layer for smoke segmentation appears not to be done (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Define the index using controlled captures (known background, added smoke, measured noise), evaluate 3-5 public models, test curve collapse and the restricted-evaluation ranking stability.
main_risk: Estimating the counterfactual background (needed for contrast change) in the wild is hard; the analysis may only be rigorous on controlled data, limiting the benchmark claim.
community_default_belief: Misses on thin smoke indicate insufficient model sensitivity that better training can fix.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Below the noise floor no training helps; without a detectability normalization, benchmarks conflate physics with learning.
fastest_falsification: Curve-collapse test on one controlled dataset and three models; no collapse falsifies the strong claim.

one_line: Fire is an emitter, not a surface: a measurable share of 'fire segmentation error' is actually the model segmenting illumination cast by fire onto smoke and walls.
problem: Segmentation ontology assumes objects reflect light; flames emit it and illuminate everything nearby, so the 'fire region' bleeds into the scene in a way surface segmentation cannot express.
core_hypothesis: A large, quantifiable fraction of false-positive fire pixels in current models lies in fire-illuminated (but not burning) regions, and this fraction grows as ambient light decreases, because the emitter/illuminated distinction requires dynamic-range headroom that dark scenes remove.
falsifiable_prediction: Stratifying false positives of public fire segmenters by an illumination-correlation score (temporal correlation of pixel intensity with flame-region intensity) will show illuminated-surface pixels dominating false positives at night; providing HDR or short-exposure input will reduce exactly this stratum and no other.
why_important: Fire-safety systems fail differently for 'glow on smoke' vs 'flame'; knowing that the error is an image-formation category error changes the fix from more data to different sensing or output ontology (emitter vs lit).
why_possibly_novel: Glow/halo false positives are anecdotally known; a quantitative decomposition of fire-segmentation error into emitter vs illuminated components using temporal correlation appears missing (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Night captures of controlled fires with synchronized short/long exposures, run public models on the long exposures, compute the illumination-correlation stratification, compare with short-exposure inputs.
main_risk: Flame and its cast illumination flicker coherently, so the correlation score may not separate them cleanly; may need spatial-gradient or spectral features as a secondary check.
community_default_belief: Fire false positives are appearance confusions (orange textures) fixable with harder negatives.
why_that_may_be_wrong: At night the dominant confusion is physically generated by the fire itself; no negative mining can remove real photons cast by real fire.
fastest_falsification: One night capture session plus the stratified false-positive analysis on existing checkpoints.

one_line: The refractive background-warp field, not appearance, is the strongest single cue for glass: predicting warp magnitude localizes glass better than direct mask regression at low data.
problem: Glass distorts the background geometrically (refraction) in a way that is invariant to glass color, lighting, and reflections, yet models are trained to map appearance to masks directly.
core_hypothesis: A model trained to predict the dense background-displacement field (supervisable in controlled or synthetic scenes) and thresholding its magnitude will localize refractive objects with better sample efficiency and better shape generalization than an equal-capacity direct mask model, because the warp cue is category-agnostic.
falsifiable_prediction: At small training-set sizes, warp-then-threshold will beat direct masking on held-out shapes; the two will converge as data grows; on flat window glass (near-zero warp) warp-based localization will fail predictably, mapping the method's validity boundary.
why_important: Identifies which physical channel carries the generalizable signal for refractive objects and predicts exactly where it must fail (flat panes), replacing 'glass is hard' with a cue-level theory.
why_possibly_novel: Refraction estimation exists in graphics and fluid measurement; using warp-field prediction as the primary localization mechanism with a stated failure boundary for segmentation appears untested (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Synthetic training with known warp fields plus a small real validation set (patterned backgrounds behind glass objects); compare sample-efficiency curves of warp-based vs direct models; verify the flat-pane failure prediction.
main_risk: Warp supervision requires textured backgrounds; textureless real scenes give no warp evidence, possibly limiting the cue to a subset of deployments.
community_default_belief: Reflection cues and object shape priors are the main signals for glass; refraction is too subtle to drive segmentation.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Refraction subtlety is a resolution question, not a signal-existence question; at modern resolutions the displacement of background texture may be the least ambiguous cue available.
fastest_falsification: Sample-efficiency comparison at one small data size on synthetic; if warp models do not win even there, the hypothesis dies.

one_line: Glass segmentation accuracy is secretly a function of camera viewpoint via specular highlight geometry, so datasets with photographer-height bias produce models with angle-dependent blind spots.
problem: Specular highlights, a major glass cue, move with viewpoint; datasets are shot mostly at human standing height and typical distances, entangling the cue with viewpoint statistics.
core_hypothesis: Model performance on the same physical glass objects varies systematically with camera elevation and azimuth (not just scale), tracking the visibility of speculars from the training viewpoint distribution; robot-height and ceiling-camera viewpoints suffer predictable drops.
falsifiable_prediction: A controlled sweep (same objects, same lighting, camera moved over a grid of heights/angles) will show accuracy varying with viewpoint far more for glass than for opaque controls, with the accuracy peak matching the estimated training viewpoint distribution; a highlight-visibility model will predict the accuracy surface.
why_important: Service robots and surveillance cameras operate exactly at the underrepresented viewpoints; the effect would be an invisible deployment failure with a clear data-collection fix.
why_possibly_novel: Viewpoint bias is studied for object recognition; connecting it mechanistically to specular geometry for transparent materials with a predictive visibility model appears new (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Tabletop grid-sweep capture with a camera arm or tripod ladder, evaluation of public glass models across the grid, regression of accuracy against a computed specular-visibility score.
main_risk: Lighting layout confounds elevation effects; needs repeated sweeps under multiple lighting configurations to isolate geometry.
community_default_belief: Viewpoint robustness for segmentation is mostly about scale and occlusion; material-specific viewpoint effects are second-order.
why_that_may_be_wrong: For materials whose evidence is mostly specular, viewpoint changes the very existence of the evidence, not just its appearance.
fastest_falsification: A coarse 3-height x 3-angle sweep on a dozen objects with one public model.

one_line: Smoke is chromatically near-neutral by scattering physics; a chromaticity-invariance test separates smoke from white solid distractors, and current models fail it.
problem: Large-particle scattering is roughly wavelength-independent, so smoke shifts pixel colors toward a neutral mixture while preserving background hue direction underneath; white objects replace hue entirely. Models are never tested on this distinction.
core_hypothesis: True smoke overlays preserve a recoverable trace of background chromaticity (hue direction persists at reduced saturation), while opaque white/gray distractors do not; a simple chromatic-consistency statistic separates the two cases, and current models' false positives on white objects are concentrated where this statistic says 'opaque'.
falsifiable_prediction: On controlled overlays (real smoke over colored backgrounds vs white cloth/wall patches), the statistic will separate classes strongly; model false positives on distractors will lie overwhelmingly in the statistic's 'opaque' region, showing the models ignore an available physical cue.
why_important: Provides a near-zero-cost physical filter for the most common smoke false alarms (steam-like whites, walls, clouds) and a diagnostic of what cues models actually use.
why_possibly_novel: Color-line and haze-line priors exist in dehazing; converting them into a falsifiable claim about the error geography of modern smoke segmenters appears new (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build the overlay set (fog machine over colored boards; white panels as controls), compute the statistic, run public models, and measure the overlap between model false positives and statistic-flagged opaque regions.
main_risk: Fire-tinted or heavily colored smoke violates neutrality; the filter's scope must be characterized as a function of smoke type.
community_default_belief: Smoke vs white-object confusion is a texture/context problem to be solved with more diverse negatives.
why_that_may_be_wrong: There is a deterministic chromatic signature distinguishing translucent neutral overlays from opaque whites; the confusion persists because the cue is absent from training objectives, not because the classes are inseparable.
fastest_falsification: Compute the statistic's class separation on one afternoon of controlled overlays; weak separation kills the premise.

one_line: Two orthogonal polarization captures may make transparent-object segmentation nearly trivial, implying the field's difficulty is an RGB-sensor artifact rather than an algorithmic frontier.
problem: Specular reflection off dielectric surfaces (glass) is strongly polarized while diffuse backgrounds are weakly polarized, yet the community benchmarks transparent segmentation almost exclusively on unpolarized RGB.
core_hypothesis: The degree-of-polarization image separates glass surfaces from background so cleanly in common indoor/outdoor conditions that a shallow classifier on two-polarization input approaches the accuracy of large RGB models, revealing that most published difficulty is sensor-induced.
falsifiable_prediction: On a paired capture set (RGB + two polarizer angles, same scenes), a small model on polarization channels will reach a large fraction of the accuracy of state-of-the-art RGB models trained on far more data; failure cases will concentrate at Brewster-angle-unfavorable geometries, as physics predicts.
why_important: If a cheap optical change collapses the problem, resources spent on architectural innovation for RGB glass segmentation are misallocated, and deployment guidance should change.
why_possibly_novel: Polarization vision for reflection removal is established; the specific claim that it trivializes segmentation to shallow-model level, with a physics-predicted failure geography, is a quantified bet that appears untested at benchmark scale (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Capture ~200 scenes with a rotatable polarizer or polarization sensor, train a small model on polarization features, compare against public RGB models on the same scenes, and map errors vs incidence-angle estimates.
main_risk: Uncontrolled outdoor illumination and multiple reflections may degrade polarization contrast badly; the claim may hold only indoors.
community_default_belief: Transparent object segmentation is an open algorithmic challenge to be solved with better networks on RGB.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The information bottleneck may be optical, not computational; the field may be optimizing decoding of a signal it discarded at the sensor.
fastest_falsification: A 20-scene pilot with a hand-rotated polarizer and logistic regression on polarization contrast.

one_line: Cast shadows of smoke are often more detectable than the smoke itself, and current models make no use of this indirect evidence.
problem: A backlit thin plume can be nearly invisible against sky while casting a high-contrast moving shadow on the ground; the evidence for the medium lies outside the medium's pixels.
core_hypothesis: In sunlit scenes there exists a measurable regime where smoke-shadow contrast exceeds direct smoke contrast, and current segmenters' predictions are causally independent of shadow evidence (masking the shadow region does not change the smoke prediction), demonstrating an unexploited information channel.
falsifiable_prediction: Occlusion tests (graying out shadow regions) will leave public models' smoke masks essentially unchanged; a detector augmented with a shadow-association channel will detect thin sunlit plumes at lower densities than any pixel-local model, in controlled outdoor releases.
why_important: Early wildfire detection at long range operates exactly in the thin-backlit regime; an ignored channel with higher SNR is a direct practical lever.
why_possibly_novel: Shadow analysis exists for opaque objects and clouds in remote sensing; ground-level smoke-shadow association as a detection channel for segmentation appears unstudied (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Outdoor fog-machine releases in low sun, measure direct vs shadow contrast across densities, run occlusion sensitivity analysis on public models, prototype a two-region association detector.
main_risk: Shadow visibility requires sun and suitable ground; the regime may be too narrow to matter operationally, which the contrast survey would reveal early.
community_default_belief: Everything needed to segment smoke lies in the smoke's own pixels plus local context.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Participating media modulate the light field globally; for optically thin media the highest-SNR evidence can be geometrically displaced from the medium.
fastest_falsification: The contrast survey plus occlusion analysis, no training required.

one_line: Beyond a computable distance, smoke and atmospheric haze are physically indistinguishable in a single image, so distant-smoke labels supervise context recognition, not medium recognition.
problem: Datasets label distant plumes (kilometers away) where the image formation of smoke converges to that of ordinary haze; what such labels teach a model is unexamined.
core_hypothesis: There is a distance/optical-depth regime where no single-image statistic separates smoke from haze (their transfer functions coincide); labels in this regime force models to rely on geographic/contextual priors (plume shape, source landmarks), which is why distant-smoke detectors transfer poorly across regions.
falsifiable_prediction: A two-alternative forced-choice test (smoke patch vs matched haze patch, context removed) will drop humans and models to chance beyond a characterizable distance band; cross-region transfer failures of distant-smoke models will concentrate on images in that band; within-band accuracy will track context availability, not patch appearance.
why_important: Defines the honest operating envelope of single-image wildfire detection and justifies temporal or multi-spectral requirements beyond it, preventing benchmarks from rewarding geographic overfitting.
why_possibly_novel: Convergence of scattering media at distance is textbook physics; using it to partition datasets into 'appearance-supervised' and 'context-supervised' subsets with transfer-failure predictions appears new (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct patch-level 2AFC sets from existing long-range imagery with distance estimates, measure human and model chance-crossing distance, then stratify cross-region transfer results by that band.
main_risk: Ground-truth distance and true class for wild imagery are hard to certify; may need controlled burns or smoke machines at surveyed distances for the anchor points.
community_default_belief: Better features will keep improving distant-smoke recognition; misses at range are a data problem.
why_that_may_be_wrong: At range the classes merge physically; further gains necessarily come from context memorization that will not transfer, so benchmark improvements in that band are illusory.
fastest_falsification: The 2AFC chance-crossing measurement on existing imagery with rough distance metadata.

one_line: Motion evidence has opposite spatial structure for smoke (dense interior texture motion) vs glass (sparse edge/specular motion), suggesting a motion-sparsity router as a unified media-segmentation front end.
problem: Smoke and transparent objects are usually treated by separate literatures, yet both are media whose main evidence under camera or scene motion is a characteristic modulation of the background; the structure of that modulation differs diagnostically.
core_hypothesis: The spatial sparsity of temporal change is a two-sided signature: volumetric media produce spatially dense, temporally decorrelating change across their support; refractive solids produce sparse, edge-concentrated, geometrically consistent change; a router computing motion-sparsity statistics can dispatch pixels to the correct downstream model and beat both single-task models on mixed scenes.
falsifiable_prediction: On videos containing both plumes and glass, the sparsity statistic will bimodally separate the two media; a routed pair of specialists will outperform each specialist alone and a jointly trained generalist of equal capacity, specifically on mixed scenes and not on single-medium scenes.
why_important: Unifies two fragmented problem areas under one measurable physical signature and offers an architecture-level hypothesis that is testable rather than aesthetic.
why_possibly_novel: Motion cues are used within each subfield; a cross-media sparsity dichotomy as an explicit routing signal appears unproposed (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute the sparsity statistics on mixed-media captures (kitchen scenes with steam and glassware; lab scenes), verify bimodality, then assemble router plus existing pretrained specialists and compare on mixed vs pure scenes.
main_risk: Camera shake and background motion inject their own change statistics; the router may need stabilization quality beyond what deployments provide.
community_default_belief: Smoke segmentation and transparent-object segmentation are unrelated tasks needing separate solutions.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Both are background-modulation problems; their difference is a low-dimensional statistic of the modulation, which is exactly the kind of thing a small front end can measure.
fastest_falsification: Bimodality check of the statistic on a handful of mixed videos.

one_line: Promptable segmenters have a boundary-snapping defect on media: mask boundaries align to background image gradients more than ground truth does, measurably hallucinating crisp edges inside smoke.
problem: Foundation segmenters are trained overwhelmingly on crisp-boundary objects; their behavior on gradient-poor diffuse boundaries is anecdotally bad but uncharacterized as a systematic bias.
core_hypothesis: For smoke regions, promptable-segmenter output boundaries co-locate with strong background gradients (building silhouettes, horizon lines seen through smoke) at rates far exceeding ground-truth boundary/gradient co-location, quantifying a specific inductive bias: the model believes boundaries live on edges.
falsifiable_prediction: A gradient-alignment score (fraction of predicted boundary pixels within a small radius of a strong image gradient) will be significantly higher for model predictions than for GT masks on smoke, the excess will grow with background clutter, and the same score on solid objects will show no excess.
why_important: Turns 'foundation models are bad at smoke' into a measurable, targetable bias with a clear remediation test (does soft-boundary fine-tuning reduce the alignment excess?).
why_possibly_novel: Failure reports on amorphous objects exist; the specific gradient-alignment excess statistic as a quantitative defect signature appears unproposed (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run public promptable segmenters on smoke datasets with varied-clutter backgrounds, compute alignment excess vs GT, correlate with clutter measures, and test whether small soft-label fine-tunes reduce it.
main_risk: GT masks themselves may partially snap to edges (annotators use the same heuristic), compressing the measurable excess; needs the controlled-capture GT from physically defined extents as a clean reference.
community_default_belief: Foundation segmenters fail on smoke because smoke is out of distribution; more diverse training data will fix it.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The failure may be a structural prior (edges equal boundaries) that data diversity alone does not remove unless the label geometry itself changes.
fastest_falsification: Alignment-excess computation on one dataset with one public model.

one_line: Point prompts 'fall through' translucent media at a rate that tracks opacity: prompt fall-through of a frozen promptable segmenter is a zero-training opacity probe.
problem: When prompted inside thin smoke or glass, promptable segmenters often return the background object instead; this is treated as failure noise rather than as a signal.
core_hypothesis: The probability that a point prompt inside a medium returns a background-object mask (fall-through rate) is a monotone function of local medium opacity, making the frozen model an unintentional opacity sensor whose output can supervise or calibrate dedicated media models.
falsifiable_prediction: On rendered and fog-machine data with known transmittance, fall-through rate estimated over prompt jitter will rank-correlate strongly with transmittance; a density map assembled from fall-through statistics will approach the quality of maps from disagreement-based supervision (idea C-011) without any annotation at all.
why_important: Provides free, scalable density pseudo-labels from an off-the-shelf frozen model, converting a documented defect into a supervision source.
why_possibly_novel: Using prompt-response instability as a measurement instrument for a physical quantity, rather than as a robustness failure, appears to be an unexplored inversion (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Grid-prompt public segmenters over controlled smoke footage, compute fall-through maps, correlate with measured transmittance, then distill a small density model from fall-through pseudo-labels and evaluate.
main_risk: Fall-through also depends on the salience of the background object; needs normalization by background-object promptability measured in smoke-free frames.
community_default_belief: Prompt instability on media is an artifact to be engineered away with better prompting or fine-tuning.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The instability is caused by the physical mixing of two signals; its statistics therefore carry the mixing ratio, which is the quantity of interest.
fastest_falsification: Fall-through vs transmittance correlation on one controlled sequence.

one_line: Different foundation models disagree about glass in characteristic ways (depth sees through it, segmenters segment behind it), and their disagreement map is itself a free glass detector.
problem: Each pretrained vision model resolves the ill-posedness of transparency according to its own training bias; these biases differ across tasks, but the structure of cross-model disagreement is unstudied.
core_hypothesis: Pixels on transparent surfaces produce a distinctive cross-model inconsistency signature (e.g. monocular depth reporting the far surface while stereo or shading cues report near; segmenters labeling the occluded object), and thresholding a cross-model inconsistency score localizes glass with accuracy competitive with weakly supervised dedicated detectors, using zero glass-specific training.
falsifiable_prediction: On transparent-object benchmarks, an inconsistency score computed from a fixed set of public frozen models (depth, segmentation, normals) will achieve localization far above chance and above any single model's implicit glass channel; ablating models from the ensemble will show the depth/segmentation disagreement carrying most of the signal.
why_important: Zero-annotation glass localization would bootstrap dataset creation and provide a diagnostic of how different training objectives encode transparency.
why_possibly_novel: Cross-model consistency has been used for uncertainty; targeting material transparency via task-specific bias disagreement appears novel as a detection mechanism (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble frozen public models, define the inconsistency score, evaluate localization on existing transparent-object data against weak baselines.
main_risk: Models increasingly share training data and distillation lineage, which may homogenize their transparency biases and erase the signal over time.
community_default_belief: Glass detection needs glass-specific supervision because generic models simply fail on it.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The models do not fail identically; the geometry of their disagreement encodes the material, so 'failing models' jointly contain the label.
fastest_falsification: Score computation and localization test on a small set of glass scenes using two frozen models.

one_line: Open-vocabulary segmenters respond to smoke's context, not smoke: text-driven 'smoke' masks are driven by chimneys, flames, and sky composition rather than the medium's pixels.
problem: Vision-language embeddings for weather/media words are trained from captions where the word co-occurs with scene context; whether the grounded region actually tracks the medium is untested.
core_hypothesis: Open-vocabulary segmentation for media terms is dominated by contextual anchors: pasting real smoke into atypical contexts (indoor office, snowfield) sharply reduces recall, while context-without-medium images (chimney with no smoke, extinguished fire scene) produce confident false masks whose spatial layout tracks where smoke 'should' be.
falsifiable_prediction: A 2x2 test (medium present/absent x typical/atypical context) will show context dominating the response variance for media classes but appearance dominating for solid classes in the same framework; false masks in context-only images will align with plausible plume geometry rather than random regions.
why_important: Open-vocabulary tools are being adopted for environmental monitoring; if they ground context, their failure mode is systematic hallucination in high-risk scenes (fire trucks present, smoke gone, alarm continues).
why_possibly_novel: Context-reliance analyses exist for classification; the 2x2 causal design applied to text-grounded segmentation of volumetric media appears new (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build the 2x2 image set via compositing and real curation, run public open-vocabulary segmenters, decompose response variance by factor.
main_risk: Compositing artifacts could leak the manipulation; needs real atypical-context smoke (fog machine indoors) as the gold condition.
community_default_belief: Text-grounded segmenters localize the named concept; errors are noise from imperfect alignment.
why_that_may_be_wrong: For concepts photographed almost exclusively in stereotyped contexts, caption supervision cannot distinguish concept from context, so the learned grounding is a scene template.
fastest_falsification: Chimney-without-smoke curation plus model runs; confident plume-shaped masks on empty chimneys is immediate evidence.

one_line: Mask decoders carry a simply-connected topology prior: predicted smoke masks have systematically lower genus (fewer holes, fewer wisp components) than ground truth, and the deficit is architecture-attributable.
problem: Smoke masks are topologically rich (holes, disconnected wisps, filaments); whether decoder architectures can even express such topology at typical output resolutions is unexamined.
core_hypothesis: The topological complexity (component count, hole count) of predicted media masks is bounded well below ground-truth complexity across current architectures, the bound tightens with decoder upsampling aggressiveness, and matching region metrics can coexist with severe topology loss, hiding the defect from standard evaluation.
falsifiable_prediction: Computing Betti-number-style statistics on predictions vs GT across architectures will show a consistent complexity deficit for media but not solids; the deficit will correlate with decoder design (upsampling ratio, query count) rather than encoder capacity; region metrics will not detect it.
why_important: Downstream uses like plume volume estimation and dispersion modeling depend on topology; a hidden expressiveness ceiling redirects effort from encoders to output parameterizations.
why_possibly_novel: Topology-aware losses exist in medical imaging; a cross-architecture audit attributing topology loss to decoder design for amorphous media appears missing (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate a diverse zoo of public segmenters on finely annotated smoke data, compute topology statistics, regress deficit on architectural covariates.
main_risk: GT topology itself is annotation-limited (idea C-010's fractal issue); conclusions must be phrased relative to annotatable topology.
community_default_belief: Architectural differences among modern decoders are minor for accuracy; encoders and data dominate outcomes.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Region metrics saturate while topology stays broken, so the community's metric choice has hidden a dimension along which decoders differ dramatically.
fastest_falsification: Topology statistics on three architecturally distinct public models over one finely annotated set.

one_line: Prompt-jitter output variance of a frozen promptable segmenter is a zero-training ambiguity meter that flags boundary-undefined objects before any task model runs.
problem: Systems need to know when a scene contains ambiguity-class objects (media, transparency) to route or abstain, but building such a detector normally requires its own labels.
core_hypothesis: The variance of masks returned by a frozen promptable segmenter under small prompt perturbations is systematically higher over ambiguous media than over solid objects, and an instability map thresholded at a single global value detects 'boundary-undefined object present' with useful accuracy across domains it was never tuned on.
falsifiable_prediction: Instability maps will separate media/transparent regions from solid regions with high AUROC on datasets from disjoint domains using one shared threshold; ablations will show the signal survives image noise and prompt-grid choices, i.e. it reflects the scene, not the measurement procedure.
why_important: A free, calibration-stable ambiguity front end enables abstention, routing, and targeted annotation without any new training, particularly valuable for safety systems.
why_possibly_novel: Ensemble/TTA variance is a known uncertainty proxy; prompt-space variance of a promptable model as a cross-domain ambiguity detector with a fixed threshold appears untested (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute instability maps on mixed datasets (media, glass, solids), measure AUROC with one global threshold, run the invariance ablations.
main_risk: Instability also fires on ordinary small/thin solid objects and cluttered textures; specificity may require a second cheap feature, complicating the 'free' claim.
community_default_belief: Detecting ambiguous-object presence requires either supervised detectors or task-specific uncertainty heads.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Foundation models already encode the ambiguity implicitly as decision instability; the information is extractable by perturbation without any training.
fastest_falsification: AUROC of instability maps on one media dataset vs one solid dataset.

one_line: Transmittance is linearly decodable from frozen self-supervised features, locating the media-segmentation bottleneck in mask heads rather than representations.
problem: It is unknown whether the failure of foundation models on smoke lives in the representation (features do not encode density) or the decision layer (features encode it, heads cannot use it).
core_hypothesis: Per-patch transmittance of smoke is decodable from frozen self-supervised ViT features by a linear map at accuracy far above chance, implying representations already contain the physical variable and the community's fine-tuning of full backbones for media is misdirected effort relative to head redesign.
falsifiable_prediction: Linear probes on frozen features will recover transmittance rank order on rendered and controlled real smoke with high correlation; probe accuracy will be flat across backbone fine-tuning (fine-tuned vs frozen), while full-model mask quality varies strongly with head design, dissociating the two factors.
why_important: Determines where scarce media-annotation budgets should go: representation adaptation vs output-space engineering, a first-order resource allocation question.
why_possibly_novel: Linear probing is standard for semantics and depth; probing for a participating-medium physical variable and using the result to arbitrate a bottleneck debate appears new (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Probe several frozen backbones on rendered transmittance data, validate on fog-machine captures, compare probe curves against mask-quality curves under head/backbone ablations.
main_risk: Either outcome could be confounded by synthetic rendering shortcuts; the real-capture validation set is mandatory, not optional.
community_default_belief: Media segmentation fails because pretrained features are not adapted to amorphous appearance; backbone fine-tuning is the remedy.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Self-supervised objectives already reward representing photometric mixing (it predicts patch appearance); the loss may be purely in the classification geometry of the head.
fastest_falsification: One linear probe on one frozen backbone with rendered data.

one_line: Interactive refinement diverges on media: additional correction clicks make smoke masks oscillate rather than converge, because click protocols presuppose a refinable boundary.
problem: Interactive segmentation assumes each correction click monotonically improves the mask; on boundary-undefined objects this assumption is untested and likely false.
