core_hypothesis: Click-based interactive models exhibit non-convergent oscillation on media (mask area and boundary position cycling with successive clicks), with oscillation amplitude tracking local ambiguity, whereas solid objects show monotone convergence; the defect is protocol-level and persists across model generations.
falsifiable_prediction: Scripted click simulations on smoke images will show non-monotone IoU trajectories and higher inter-click mask churn than solids, across multiple public interactive models; human-in-the-loop sessions will show more clicks spent on smoke with worse final satisfaction ratings, replicating the simulation.
why_important: Interactive tools are the assumed fallback for hard annotation; if they structurally fail on media, annotation cost models and dataset plans built on them are wrong.
why_possibly_novel: Click-count benchmarks exist; convergence/oscillation analysis as a protocol-level failure signature for boundary-undefined objects appears unexamined (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run standard click-simulation protocols on media vs solid datasets across public interactive models, measure trajectory monotonicity and churn; small human study for the applied claim.
main_risk: Click simulators encode boundary assumptions themselves; the human study is needed to avoid circularity, adding cost.
community_default_belief: Interactive segmentation handles hard cases; enough clicks always recover a good mask.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Clicks are point evidence about a boundary; where no boundary exists, each click resolves ambiguity locally while re-raising it elsewhere, a fixed-point failure rather than a slow convergence.
fastest_falsification: Click-simulation trajectories on one interactive model over one smoke set.

one_line: Fire segmentation competence is bimodal across illumination (easy at night, hard in daylight), and single aggregate benchmark scores conceal that models fail exactly when visual confirmation matters.
problem: Flame contrast regime flips between day (translucent flame against lit scene) and night (dominant emitter); benchmarks aggregate over an uncontrolled illumination mix, producing meaningless averages.
core_hypothesis: Public fire segmenters' per-image accuracy distribution is strongly bimodal with illumination as the latent factor; day-condition accuracy is far lower than the aggregate suggests, and cross-dataset ranking of methods changes when scores are conditioned on illumination, meaning current leaderboards partially rank datasets' day/night mixes rather than models.
falsifiable_prediction: Stratifying existing benchmark results by an estimated illumination index will reveal a large day-night gap consistent across models, plus at least one method-pair whose ranking inverts between strata; controlling the mix will reproduce or erase headline gaps between methods.
why_important: Fire-safety procurement decisions ride on these scores; a mix-dependent leaderboard is actively misleading for daytime-critical deployments like industrial monitoring.
why_possibly_novel: Day/night difficulty is folklore; demonstrating rank inversion under stratification and quantifying the mix-sensitivity of published-style comparisons appears undone (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute illumination indices for existing fire datasets, re-score public models per stratum, test for bimodality and rank inversion.
main_risk: Illumination estimation from images is imperfect; needs a hand-verified subset to calibrate the strata.
community_default_belief: A single mIoU/F-score per dataset fairly summarizes a fire segmenter's quality.
why_that_may_be_wrong: When difficulty is bimodal in a latent factor with dataset-dependent mixing proportions, aggregate scores are non-comparable across datasets and unstable across deployments.
fastest_falsification: Stratified re-scoring of two public models on one dataset with day/night metadata.

one_line: Appearance-template video trackers have a computable half-life on smoke set by turbulent decorrelation, so tracking failure is a physical timescale, not a model deficiency.
problem: Video object segmentation on smoke is reported as unstable, but instability is attributed to model weakness rather than to the target's intrinsic appearance decorrelation rate.
core_hypothesis: The time for a smoke region's appearance to decorrelate below trackers' matching thresholds is a measurable physical quantity (a function of turbulence intensity and viewing scale), and tracker persistence on smoke is predicted by this half-life across models: no appearance-matching tracker exceeds it, while motion-integration methods can.
falsifiable_prediction: Measured appearance-autocorrelation half-lives of smoke regions will predict time-to-loss for multiple public video segmenters (strong correlation across clips), rescaling with playback speed manipulations exactly as the physical account demands; models with explicit flow integration will violate the bound.
why_important: Establishes a principled performance ceiling for a whole model family on media, preventing wasted iteration and pointing to which architectural ingredient (motion integration) actually changes the ceiling.
why_possibly_novel: Appearance-decorrelation as a predictive law for tracker lifetime on turbulent media, with the playback-speed rescaling test, appears unformulated (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute patch autocorrelation timescales on smoke clips, run public video segmenters, correlate time-to-loss with half-life, then rerun at altered playback speeds.
main_risk: Trackers differ in re-detection heuristics that can mask the underlying matching failure; analysis must separate initial loss from recovery behavior.
community_default_belief: Better video foundation models will steadily fix smoke tracking as capacity and data grow.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The failure is set by the target's physics interacting with the appearance-matching mechanism itself; scaling the mechanism cannot cross a decorrelation-imposed bound.
fastest_falsification: Half-life vs time-to-loss correlation on a dozen clips with one tracker.

one_line: IoU and matting metrics rank smoke models differently as a matter of course, so 'state of the art' in smoke segmentation is metric-relative in a way the field has not acknowledged.
problem: Model comparisons on media inherit IoU from solid-object segmentation without checking whether soft-boundary-appropriate metrics (alpha error, connectivity-aware measures) would order methods the same way.
core_hypothesis: Across a pool of public smoke segmenters, rank correlation between IoU-based orderings and soft/matting-based orderings is low enough that several published-style superiority claims would invert, and the divergence concentrates in models differing in boundary behavior rather than region behavior.
falsifiable_prediction: Evaluating the same model pool under both metric families on datasets with soft or multi-annotator labels will produce rank correlations well below what is seen for solid-object tasks, with identifiable inversion pairs; the inversions will be attributable to boundary-band pixels by decomposition.
why_important: If method ranking is metric-fragile, the field's progress narrative on smoke is partly an artifact of an inherited metric, and benchmark maintainers need to publish multi-metric results.
why_possibly_novel: Metric-sensitivity studies exist for saliency and matting; a systematic rank-stability audit specifically for smoke/fire segmentation appears missing (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble public checkpoints, evaluate under both families on soft-labeled data, compute rank correlations and locate inversions via boundary-band decomposition.
main_risk: Soft labels at scale are scarce; may require the controlled-capture datasets proposed elsewhere in this shard, coupling this idea's testability to dataset work.
community_default_belief: IoU differences reflect real quality differences; metric choice is a technicality.
why_that_may_be_wrong: For soft objects, IoU differences within the boundary band mostly measure threshold placement, which is exactly the quantity that has no ground truth (idea C-001).
fastest_falsification: Two-metric evaluation of five checkpoints on one soft-labeled dataset.

one_line: Boundary-tolerance metrics on smoke change model rankings when evaluation resolution changes, because tolerance radii interact with non-converging fractal boundaries.
problem: Boundary F-style metrics fix a pixel tolerance that silently changes physical meaning across resolutions; for fractal-like media boundaries this is not a benign rescaling.
core_hypothesis: For smoke, the model ranking induced by boundary-tolerance metrics is unstable across evaluation resolutions (rank inversions occur between common resolution choices), while solid-object rankings are stable, and the instability magnitude is predicted by the boundary's measured scale complexity.
falsifiable_prediction: Re-evaluating a fixed model pool at multiple resolutions will produce systematically lower cross-resolution rank correlation for smoke than for a solid-object control task; per-image instability will correlate with box-counting complexity of the GT boundary.
why_important: Papers evaluate at heterogeneous resolutions; if rankings do not transfer across resolution for media, cross-paper comparisons are invalid and a scale-explicit metric standard is needed.
why_possibly_novel: Resolution sensitivity of boundary metrics is known qualitatively; tying instability quantitatively to boundary fractal statistics and demonstrating rank inversion on media appears new (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Multi-resolution re-evaluation of public models on one smoke and one solid dataset, rank-correlation analysis, complexity regression.
main_risk: Resampling artifacts of GT masks at different resolutions must be handled carefully or they will manufacture the effect being tested.
community_default_belief: Boundary metrics with standard tolerances fairly compare fine mask quality at any reasonable resolution.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The metric's tolerance is an implicit scale parameter; on scale-free boundaries there is no resolution at which it becomes canonical.
fastest_falsification: Three-resolution evaluation of three models on one smoke set.

one_line: Human judges prefer physically plausible smoke masks over pixel-accurate ones, so IoU optimization and perceived quality diverge for media in a way they do not for solids.
problem: It is assumed that higher-IoU masks look better; for amorphous objects a mask can be pixelwise closer to GT while violating plume physics (impossible shapes, broken connectivity), and no one has measured the divergence.
core_hypothesis: In forced-choice comparisons, human preference between competing smoke masks disagrees with IoU ordering at a substantial rate, and the disagreement is predicted by plausibility features (connectivity to source, smooth density gradients, flow alignment) that IoU ignores.
falsifiable_prediction: A paired-preference study over model outputs will show preference-IoU disagreement significantly more often for smoke than for a solid-object control; a plausibility feature set will predict the disagreement cases with high accuracy.
why_important: Human operators consume these masks in monitoring settings; optimizing a metric anti-correlated with operator trust in a known case class undermines deployed usefulness.
why_possibly_novel: Perceptual-metric divergence is documented for image synthesis; establishing it for media segmentation and identifying physics-plausibility as the mediating factor appears new (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect pairwise human preferences on a few hundred mask pairs spanning IoU gaps, fit disagreement predictors, compare smoke vs solid control.
main_risk: Preferences may be driven by superficial aesthetics (smoothness) rather than physics; the feature analysis must include smoothness-only baselines.
community_default_belief: IoU improvements translate to better masks for all downstream consumers, human or machine.
why_that_may_be_wrong: IoU is indifferent to physical coherence; for objects defined by their generative physics, humans judge coherence first and pixel overlap second.
fastest_falsification: A small preference pilot (50 pairs, 10 raters) against IoU ordering.

one_line: Benchmarks should weight errors by physical detectability: unweighted scores on smoke largely measure how well models memorize labels on undetectable pixels.
problem: A substantial fraction of labeled smoke pixels may lie below any single-image detectability threshold (idea C-020); scoring them equally with detectable pixels contaminates the measurement of actual competence.
core_hypothesis: Re-weighting benchmark pixels by a detectability index will change both the absolute scores and the relative ranking of methods, and the methods that gain most under detectability weighting are those that generalize best to new domains, because unweighted scores partly reward label memorization strategies.
falsifiable_prediction: Detectability-weighted re-scoring will produce rank changes among public models; cross-dataset generalization performance will correlate better with weighted scores than with unweighted scores.
why_important: Gives benchmark maintainers a concrete, physics-based fix that makes leaderboards predictive of deployment rather than of test-set idiosyncrasy.
why_possibly_novel: Difficulty-weighted evaluation exists in various forms; deriving weights from an image-formation detectability model for media, and validating them against transfer performance, appears untried (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement the index on datasets with adequate metadata (or controlled captures), re-score a model pool, correlate weighted/unweighted scores with cross-dataset transfer results.
main_risk: The detectability index itself embeds modeling choices; adversaries of the idea can attribute rank changes to index bias, so index-robustness checks across formulations are needed.
community_default_belief: All labeled pixels are equally legitimate test points; weighting schemes are unnecessary complications.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Pixels carrying no signal cannot measure perception; scoring them measures the prior a model applies where evidence is absent, an entirely different competence.
fastest_falsification: Weighted vs unweighted rank comparison on one dataset with one index formulation.

one_line: Most of the cross-dataset 'domain gap' in smoke segmentation is annotation-protocol gap: re-annotating a test set under the training set's protocol recovers a majority of the lost performance.
problem: Cross-dataset drops are automatically attributed to visual domain shift; for media, the labeling rules (what counts as smoke, threshold strictness, tool, instance conventions) differ at least as much as the pixels.
core_hypothesis: For smoke datasets, a controlled protocol-swap (re-annotating a sample of dataset B's images under dataset A's exact written protocol and annotator training) will recover a large fraction of the cross-dataset performance drop of models trained on A, demonstrating that the measured gap is substantially a supervision-definition gap.
falsifiable_prediction: The protocol-swap recovery fraction will be significantly higher for smoke/fire than for a solid-object class pair with analogous dataset pairs; recovery will be largest in boundary-band and thin-smoke pixels.
why_important: Domain adaptation research on media may be optimizing against a mislabeled cause; the finding would redirect effort toward protocol standardization and label translation rather than feature alignment.
why_possibly_novel: Cross-dataset label inconsistency is known in principle; a quantitative protocol-swap decomposition of the media domain gap appears missing (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Pick two smoke datasets with published protocols, re-annotate a few hundred images of each under the other's protocol, evaluate pretrained models against both label versions, compute recovery fractions.
main_risk: Protocols are often under-documented; reconstructing them faithfully may require contacting original teams, and imperfect reconstruction biases toward under-estimating recovery.
community_default_belief: Cross-dataset performance drops measure visual domain shift that adaptation methods should address.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The test labels changed along with the pixels; without holding the label function fixed, the drop confounds two causes, plausibly dominated by the label function for ambiguous classes.
fastest_falsification: Protocol-swap on 100 images of one dataset pair.

one_line: Benchmark scores for smoke segmentation are uncorrelated with false-alarm rates on smoke-like distractors, because positive-heavy collection made distractors statistically invisible to evaluation.
problem: Deployment cost is dominated by false alarms on steam, fog, dust, clouds, glare, and exhaust, but datasets collected by searching for smoke contain few hard negatives, so metrics cannot see the failure that matters.
core_hypothesis: Across public models, standard benchmark scores and false-alarm rates on a purpose-built distractor suite are essentially uncorrelated (or weakly anti-correlated, if aggressive models win benchmarks), meaning model selection by benchmark actively fails to select for deployability.
falsifiable_prediction: Ranking a model pool by benchmark score and separately by distractor false-alarm rate will yield near-zero rank correlation; adding a modest distractor set to training will dramatically change the second ranking while barely moving the first.
why_important: The result would show the field's selection signal is orthogonal to the deployment objective for this task class, an actionable indictment with a cheap remedy (mandatory distractor tracks).
why_possibly_novel: Hard-negative gaps are acknowledged qualitatively; measuring the rank decorrelation between benchmark and distractor performance for media segmentation appears undone (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Curate a distractor suite from real footage categories (steam vents, fog banks, dust plumes, cloud shadows, lens flare), evaluate public checkpoints, compute rank correlations against their benchmark scores.
main_risk: Distractor suite curation embeds its own distribution choices; needs category-stratified reporting to avoid replacing one arbitrary aggregate with another.
community_default_belief: Higher benchmark scores indicate models that will also false-alarm less in the field.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Benchmarks measure discrimination on the collected distribution; false alarms live on a disjoint distribution that collection pipelines systematically excluded.
fastest_falsification: Evaluate three checkpoints on one afternoon-curated distractor set and compare orderings.

one_line: Temporal-consistency metrics penalize physically correct behavior on smoke: real plume boundaries change faster than the smoothness these metrics reward.
problem: Video segmentation metrics penalize frame-to-frame mask change ('flicker') without asking how fast the underlying object legitimately changes; for turbulent media, high change rates are ground truth.
core_hypothesis: The frame-to-frame mask change rate of true smoke extents (measurable in controlled captures) exceeds the implicit stability preference of common temporal-consistency metrics, so models optimized for those metrics systematically lag real plume evolution, and the lag is detectable as a directional phase delay in growing plumes.
falsifiable_prediction: Models with better temporal-consistency scores will show larger measured phase lag against controlled growing plumes; a physically calibrated consistency metric (change rate normalized by flow-warped expected change) will invert some model rankings and eliminate the lag-rewarding behavior.
why_important: Early-warning latency is the key operational quantity; a metric that rewards lag is optimizing against the mission while appearing to improve quality.
why_possibly_novel: Flicker metrics are debated in video segmentation generally; demonstrating a physically induced conflict with a calibrated alternative for media appears new (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Controlled growing-plume captures with dense GT, evaluate public video models for consistency scores and phase lag, test the calibrated metric's ranking behavior.
main_risk: Optical-flow estimation inside smoke is unreliable, complicating the calibrated metric's normalization term; may need controlled-scene flow from marker particles.
community_default_belief: Temporal smoothness of predicted masks is an unambiguous virtue for video segmentation.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Smoothness priors encode solid-object dynamics; media violate them by nature, so the prior becomes a systematic error injected by the metric.
fastest_falsification: Phase-lag measurement of one consistency-optimized model on one controlled growing plume.

one_line: Instance-level metrics (AP, panoptic quality) are undefined-in-practice for plumes because plume countability is unstable: the metric variance induced by arbitrary instance conventions exceeds model differences.
problem: Plumes merge, split, and have no canonical individuation, yet instance and panoptic metrics require a fixed instance decomposition; the sensitivity of scores to that arbitrary choice is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: Re-annotating the same smoke scenes under different defensible instance conventions (split-by-source, split-by-connectivity, single-media-region) changes instance-metric scores of fixed models by more than typical inter-model gaps, demonstrating that instance metrics on media measure convention agreement rather than model quality.
falsifiable_prediction: Score spreads across instance conventions will exceed the spread across models for smoke, while for a things-class control the convention-induced spread will be small; models ranked under one convention will re-rank under another.
why_important: Panoptic-style benchmarks increasingly include media classes; if scores there are convention artifacts, conclusions drawn from them about model progress are unfounded.
why_possibly_novel: Instance ambiguity for stuff-like classes is acknowledged; a quantitative convention-sensitivity audit showing convention variance dominating model variance appears missing (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Triple-convention re-annotation of a few dozen multi-plume scenes, evaluation of a model pool under each, variance decomposition of scores.
main_risk: Constructing all conventions honestly requires care to avoid a strawman convention that manufactures the effect.
community_default_belief: Panoptic metrics extend naturally to all classes, including amorphous ones, with instances defined by connectivity.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Connectivity of turbulent media is a fast-changing, resolution-dependent property, so the induced instances are unstable measurement artifacts, not objects.
fastest_falsification: Two-convention scoring of two models on a dozen multi-plume scenes.

one_line: Construct validity for smoke segmentation can be tested by correlating mask outputs with independently measured physical quantities, and current models may fail the test their metrics never apply.
problem: Segmentation quality is defined circularly against human masks; whether 'good segmentation' tracks any physical property of the actual smoke (emission rate, optical depth, plume volume) is unknown.
core_hypothesis: In controlled scenes where physical smoke quantities are measured (metered fog output, transmissometer readings), the correlation between model mask statistics and physical quantities is low for models with top label-based scores, and the two evaluation axes (label agreement vs physical correlation) identify different best models.
falsifiable_prediction: Across a model pool, label-metric ranking and physical-correlation ranking will disagree substantially; some models will show high label scores with near-zero incremental physical correlation beyond mask area, exposing label-fitting without physical grounding.
why_important: Applications consume masks as physical proxies (how much smoke, growing or shrinking); construct validity is the missing audit between benchmark success and application usefulness.
why_possibly_novel: Construct validity language from measurement theory is rarely applied to segmentation; a physically instrumented validity study for media appears absent (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Instrumented fog-machine sessions with metered output and a transmissometer path, run model pool, compute both ranking axes.
main_risk: Physical measurements sample sparse points/paths while masks are dense; the mapping between them needs a defensible aggregation model or the correlation is ill-defined.
community_default_belief: Agreement with human masks is the definition of segmentation quality; physical grounding is out of scope.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Human masks are threshold artifacts (C-001); agreement with them can be maximized while tracking the underlying physical field arbitrarily badly.
fastest_falsification: Single instrumented session, three models, two correlation computations.

one_line: Glass segmentation generalization claims are confounded by object-category leakage: models detect cups and windows, not the material, and shape-novel glass exposes it.
problem: Transparent-object datasets are dominated by a few object categories; test splits share categories with training, so material understanding and category recognition are never separated.
core_hypothesis: Public glass segmenters' performance on category-novel transparent objects (irregular glass art, laboratory apparatus, unusual industrial parts) drops far more than on held-out instances of familiar categories, and a category classifier trained on their intermediate features achieves high accuracy, together demonstrating that current 'material' models are substantially category models.
falsifiable_prediction: The category-novel drop will greatly exceed the instance-novel drop; feature-space category decodability will correlate with the drop across model variants; opaque-replica controls (same shapes, painted) will show smaller category-novelty penalties, isolating the material component.
why_important: If material competence is an illusion of category coverage, robotics and safety users cannot trust deployment on unfamiliar transparent objects, and dataset design must enforce category-disjoint evaluation.
why_possibly_novel: Category bias is a known dataset issue; the paired opaque-replica control to isolate material vs category competence for transparency appears novel as a design (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble a small category-novel glass test set plus painted replicas, evaluate public models on both, run the feature decodability probe.
main_risk: Acquiring matched painted replicas is laborious; 3D-printed shape twins may substitute but change surface statistics.
community_default_belief: Good scores on held-out transparent-object test sets demonstrate material-level understanding of transparency.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Held-out splits preserve category composition; a model can score highly by recognizing cup-ness while knowing nothing about refraction or transmission.
fastest_falsification: Evaluate one public model on a dozen category-novel glass items; a large drop is immediate signal.

one_line: A tiny temporal-statistics model (two-frame differences plus local variance dynamics) can rival large single-frame networks at smoke-vs-white-distractor discrimination, showing the task's information lives in time, not appearance.
problem: The field scales spatial appearance models for smoke while the physically distinctive property of smoke is its temporal texture; the relative information content of the two channels has never been measured head-to-head.
core_hypothesis: For the specific discrimination that causes most false alarms (smoke vs static white/gray surfaces and slow clouds), a model restricted to simple temporal statistics over short windows achieves discrimination competitive with orders-of-magnitude larger single-frame models, because the discriminative mutual information is concentrated in temporal dynamics.
falsifiable_prediction: On matched evaluation (same scenes, same labels), the temporal-statistics model will approach or exceed single-frame networks on smoke-vs-distractor discrimination while losing badly on smoke-vs-textured-motion discrimination (vegetation, water), mapping where temporal information is and is not sufficient.
why_important: Reframes the efficiency frontier: if a near-trivial temporal front end covers the dominant error class, edge deployments can be dramatically cheaper, and appearance scaling is revealed as solving the wrong subproblem.
why_possibly_novel: Classical motion-based smoke detection predates deep learning; the specific information-partition claim, tested against modern large models with a stated failure domain, appears unexamined in the current era (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build the small temporal model, evaluate both model classes on a distractor-stratified video benchmark assembled from public footage, report discrimination per stratum.
main_risk: Camera motion and compression can destroy the temporal statistics; results may bifurcate by video source quality, complicating the claim.
community_default_belief: Progress on smoke detection comes from stronger spatial backbones and more data; temporal cues are auxiliary.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The physically unique signature of a participating medium in motion is temporal decorrelation of transmitted background, which single frames cannot contain at all.
fastest_falsification: Head-to-head on one stratified evaluation set; if the small model is not competitive on the distractor stratum, the strong claim dies.

one_line: The temporal power spectrum of pixel intensities inside smoke follows a characteristic turbulence-cascade slope that distinguishes it from vegetation motion, water, and flags, providing a physics-anchored feature no dataset shift can remove.
problem: Learned motion features for smoke are dataset-dependent; a physically invariant temporal signature, if it exists, would transfer by construction, but nobody has characterized one across media and distractors.
core_hypothesis: Intensity time series within smoke regions exhibit spectral slopes in a characteristic band (inherited from turbulent advection of density fluctuations) that are measurably distinct from the spectra of oscillatory distractors (vegetation: peaked; water: different slope; flags: harmonic), and the slope feature transfers across cameras and scenes with minimal recalibration.
falsifiable_prediction: Spectral-slope distributions measured across labeled regions of diverse videos will separate smoke from each distractor class with high AUROC using one global threshold band; the separation will persist across frame rates after proper frequency normalization, unlike learned features which will degrade.
why_important: A transferable physical feature would provide a robustness anchor for deployed systems and a falsifiable account of what motion-based methods implicitly learn.
why_possibly_novel: Turbulence spectra are classical physics; systematic measurement of their discriminative reach against modern distractor classes in ordinary video appears not to have been done (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Extract per-region temporal spectra from labeled public videos across classes, fit slopes, quantify separation and cross-camera stability.
main_risk: Video compression and auto-exposure inject their own temporal structure that may swamp the physical spectrum at consumer bitrates.
community_default_belief: Discriminative motion features must be learned end-to-end; hand-derived physical features were superseded for good reason.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Learned features entangle physics with camera and dataset idiosyncrasies; the physics-only component may carry most of the transferable part, which has never been isolated and measured.
fastest_falsification: Slope-distribution separation analysis on a few dozen labeled clips per class.

one_line: Optical-flow divergence is signed by plume physics: young expanding smoke shows positive flow divergence usable as a free weak label distinguishing emission sources from drifting media.
problem: Smoke segmentation treats all smoke pixels alike, but applications care most about active sources; no cheap signal currently separates actively emitting regions from residual drift.
core_hypothesis: The divergence field of optical flow within smoke regions is systematically positive near active sources (volumetric expansion projected to the image) and near zero in passively advected smoke, providing an unsupervised active-source indicator with predictable failure under strong wind shear.
falsifiable_prediction: On controlled releases with known emission schedules, flow-divergence statistics will discriminate active-emission periods from post-emission drift within the same scene; the discrimination will degrade with measured crosswind exactly as the projection geometry predicts.
why_important: Active-source localization is the actionable output for fire response and industrial leak monitoring; deriving it without labels would upgrade every existing pipeline.
why_possibly_novel: Flow statistics inside media are used for detection generally; the signed-divergence-as-emission-state hypothesis with a wind-dependent validity envelope appears unformulated (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fog-machine sessions with logged on/off schedule and anemometer, compute divergence statistics per period, fit discrimination vs wind speed.
main_risk: Optical flow inside low-texture smoke is noisy; divergence, a derivative quantity, amplifies that noise and may need aggressive spatial aggregation to stabilize.
community_default_belief: Distinguishing active sources from drifting smoke requires temporal accumulation models or human review.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The distinction is kinematic and locally measurable: expansion versus pure advection differ in first-order flow structure, which never required labels.
fastest_falsification: On/off discrimination from divergence statistics in one controlled session.

one_line: Reported flame-flicker frequency cues are partly camera artifacts: flicker features measured through rolling shutter, auto-gain, and compression do not survive sensor swaps, undermining a classical fire-detection assumption.
problem: Flicker-frequency features are a long-standing staple of video fire detection, but the measurement chain (shutter mode, gain control, codec) actively shapes temporal signals, and cross-sensor validity has not been rigorously audited.
core_hypothesis: A substantial part of the flicker signal exploited by classical and learned fire detectors is generated or reshaped by the camera pipeline; the same physical fires filmed simultaneously by different sensor/codec chains will yield flicker statistics different enough to flip detector decisions, revealing sensor overfitting where physics was assumed.
falsifiable_prediction: Simultaneous multi-camera recordings of identical fires will show flicker-band energy varying across sensor chains by more than it varies across different fires on one chain; detectors relying on flicker will disagree across chains on the same fire at a high rate.
why_important: Fire detectors are certified on one hardware set and deployed on another; a sensor-borne feature masquerading as physics is a latent safety failure with regulatory implications.
why_possibly_novel: Flicker cues are widely assumed physical; a controlled sensor-chain decomposition of the flicker signal appears missing from the fire-detection conversation (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Rig three different camera chains side by side, record controlled fires, compare flicker spectra and detector outputs across chains vs across fires.
main_risk: Perfect synchronization and identical viewpoints are hard; small geometric differences could contaminate the comparison and must be bounded with static flame-free controls.
community_default_belief: Flame flicker in a characteristic frequency band is a robust physical signature usable across cameras.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The band overlaps the temporal transfer functions of common shutter and codec machinery, so the measured signature confounds source physics with the measurement device.
fastest_falsification: Two-camera simultaneous capture of one fire; large cross-chain spectral divergence is immediate evidence.

one_line: Gravity-alignment of motion separates the white-media family: smoke rises or drifts, steam rises then vanishes, water spray falls; a reference-direction prior distinguishes classes appearance cannot.
problem: Smoke, steam, spray, and dust are nearly identical in single-frame appearance; models confuse them, yet each has a distinct signed relationship to gravity and wind that goes unused.
core_hypothesis: The distribution of vertical motion components (relative to a gravity direction available from image or metadata) differs diagnostically between buoyant media (smoke, steam: net upward near source), ballistic media (spray: net downward), and neutral media (dust: wind-locked), enabling a class disambiguation that improves false-alarm rates without any appearance retraining.
falsifiable_prediction: On labeled clips of the four classes, vertical-motion statistics will yield class separation well above appearance-model confusion rates for the same pairs; augmenting an existing model with the motion prior will cut steam/spray false alarms substantially while leaving smoke recall intact; windy scenes will degrade the separation as predicted.
why_important: Steam and spray are the top benign triggers in industrial and urban settings; a metadata-cheap physical disambiguator addresses the deployment pain point directly.
why_possibly_novel: Buoyancy is obvious qualitatively; a quantitative cross-class motion-direction study and prior-injection evaluation appears not to exist for this family (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Curate labeled clips per class, compute vertical-motion distributions, evaluate pairwise separation, then wrap the prior around one public model.
main_risk: Indoor ventilation and thermal drafts scramble motion directions; the prior's envelope may be limited to calm or outdoor conditions.
community_default_belief: White-media confusion is an appearance problem requiring more diverse training data per class.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The classes are defined physically by their transport regime, not their appearance; the discriminative axis was never in the pixels of one frame.
fastest_falsification: Vertical-motion histograms per class from a few dozen clips each.

one_line: Temporal frame averaging has opposite effects on smoke visibility depending on background dynamics, and the crossover is computable, enabling an adaptive pre-filter that beats any fixed temporal window.
problem: Preprocessing for smoke video uses fixed temporal windows; whether integration helps or hurts depends on whether it suppresses background motion noise faster than it dilutes smoke contrast, a tradeoff nobody has formalized.
core_hypothesis: Averaging N frames increases smoke detectability against dynamic backgrounds (noise suppression wins) but decreases it against static backgrounds when smoke itself moves (contrast dilution wins); the optimal N per region is predictable from local background temporal variance and smoke drift rate, and an adaptive-N front end improves any downstream detector.
falsifiable_prediction: Detectability-vs-N curves measured on controlled composites will be increasing for dynamic backgrounds and decreasing for static ones with a characterizable crossover; the adaptive front end will beat every fixed-N variant across a mixed evaluation set for multiple downstream models.
why_important: A model-agnostic preprocessing law would transfer to every smoke pipeline at negligible cost, and the crossover analysis clarifies contradictory anecdotes about temporal aggregation.
why_possibly_novel: Temporal integration is folk practice; deriving and validating the region-adaptive optimum from measurable scene statistics appears new for media detection (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct controlled composites spanning background dynamics, sweep N, fit the crossover law, implement adaptive-N, benchmark with two public detectors.
main_risk: The law may depend on smoke velocity, which is unknown a priori in deployment; a conservative estimator might erase most of the gain.
community_default_belief: More temporal context monotonically helps video detection; window size is a tuning detail.
why_that_may_be_wrong: For translucent moving targets, integration is a low-pass filter applied to the target as well as the noise; the sign of the net effect is scene-dependent, not universal.
fastest_falsification: Detectability-vs-N curves on a handful of controlled composites.

one_line: Deliberate camera micro-motion converts glass segmentation from an appearance problem into a geometry problem: induced parallax makes refractive distortion time-varying and thus directly observable.
problem: Static monocular glass segmentation is fundamentally starved of evidence, yet deployed cameras (robots, phones) can move slightly on command; the value of intentional micro-motion for transparency has not been quantified.
core_hypothesis: Sub-centimeter camera translations create background-motion anomalies at refractive surfaces (displacement fields inconsistent with any rigid scene interpretation) that are far easier to detect than static appearance cues, so active micro-motion plus a rigidity-violation test outperforms static state-of-the-art on the same scenes at a fraction of model size.
falsifiable_prediction: Paired static vs micro-motion captures of identical scenes will show large localization gains from the rigidity-violation channel; gains will vanish for flat windows viewed head-on (near-zero differential refraction) and grow with surface curvature, following the optics.
why_important: Turns an assumed-hard perception problem into a cheap active-sensing problem for the large class of platforms that can move, redefining where passive methods are actually needed.
why_possibly_novel: Structure-from-motion anomalies for transparency exist in graphics contexts; framing commanded micro-motion as the primary segmentation mechanism with a curvature-dependent validity law appears untested (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Motorized-slider captures of glass scenes with and without motion, implement the rigidity-violation detector, compare against public static models, verify the curvature dependence.
main_risk: Scene motion (people, foliage) also violates rigidity; disambiguating refractive from dynamic violations may need the very appearance cues the method tried to avoid.
community_default_belief: Glass segmentation is a passive perception problem to be solved with better single-image models.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The information deficit is in the passive data, not the model; a millimeter of motion adds a physically orthogonal evidence channel no passive scaling can create.
fastest_falsification: One slider rig session comparing static vs micro-motion localization on a few scenes.

one_line: Propagated smoke labels in video expire on a measurable timescale (label half-life), and dataset quality is bounded by the ratio of annotation refresh interval to that half-life.
problem: Video datasets economize by annotating keyframes and propagating masks, implicitly assuming labels stay valid between keyframes; for turbulent media the validity decay is fast and unquantified.
core_hypothesis: The IoU between a propagated smoke mask and the true extent decays approximately exponentially with time offset at a rate set by turbulence and flow speed; datasets whose keyframe interval exceeds the derived half-life contain a predictable fraction of stale labels, and model errors on those datasets concentrate at large offsets from keyframes.
falsifiable_prediction: Densely annotated control clips will yield measurable half-lives; for public propagated-label datasets, model error will correlate with frame distance from the nearest keyframe, and the correlation magnitude will match the staleness fraction predicted from the half-life.
why_important: Provides dataset builders a quantitative law for choosing keyframe intervals per scene type, replacing convention with measurement, and explains a hidden component of label noise in existing video benchmarks.
why_possibly_novel: Label propagation error is known qualitatively; an explicit decay-law formulation with dataset-audit predictions for media appears new (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Densely annotate a few clips spanning wind conditions, fit decay curves, then audit a propagated-label dataset for the keyframe-distance error correlation.
main_risk: Half-life likely varies strongly within a clip (near source vs downstream), so a single-parameter law may fit poorly and need spatial stratification.
community_default_belief: Keyframe propagation with human spot checks produces video labels of near-keyframe quality throughout.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Turbulent boundaries decorrelate in seconds; between keyframes the labels describe a plume that no longer exists.
fastest_falsification: Decay-curve fit on one densely annotated windy clip.

one_line: Pixelwise thermal-visible disagreement is nearly a direct glass label (opaque in long-wave infrared, transparent in visible), reducing glass detection to cheap cross-modal comparison.
problem: Glass is a hard segmentation target in visible light but is opaque and often reflective in long-wave infrared; the systematic disagreement between the two modalities at glass surfaces is unexploited as a direct signal.
core_hypothesis: A simple disagreement functional between co-registered thermal and visible views (edges present in one and absent in the other, depth-of-content mismatch) localizes glass surfaces with accuracy competitive with supervised visible-only models, while requiring no glass annotations, and its residual errors are complementary to visible-model errors.
falsifiable_prediction: On a paired thermal-visible capture set, the unsupervised disagreement map will achieve strong localization; fusing it with a visible model will correct a disproportionate share of the visible model's false negatives on clean flat glass, the visible modality's known blind spot.
why_important: Thermal sensors are increasingly cheap; if cross-modal disagreement solves the hardest visible-light failure mode, system designers gain a robust path that sidesteps years of visible-only research difficulty.
why_possibly_novel: Thermal-visible fusion exists for detection of people and vehicles; positioning modality disagreement itself as the glass signal, rather than fusing features for a supervised task, appears under-explored (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect co-registered pairs across indoor/outdoor glass scenes, implement the disagreement functional, benchmark against public visible-only models on the same scenes.
main_risk: Thermal reflections (glass acting as an infrared mirror) create structured content in the thermal view that may defeat naive disagreement measures; the functional may need reflection-awareness.
community_default_belief: Glass segmentation is a visible-spectrum computer-vision problem to be solved with better models and more labels.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The definition of the difficulty is spectral: the material's transparency is a function of wavelength, so changing wavelength dissolves the problem rather than solving it.
fastest_falsification: Disagreement-map localization on a dozen co-registered scenes.

one_line: The assumed thermal advantage for smoke segmentation may be a fire-proximity artifact: for cool or aged smoke, thermal contributes little, and reported fusion gains may vanish.
problem: Thermal-visible fusion is widely assumed beneficial for smoke because smoke is associated with fire, but much real smoke (aged, distant, cool sources) is at ambient temperature; the fusion literature rarely separates these regimes.
core_hypothesis: Fusion gains for smoke segmentation are concentrated in scenes where hot sources or heated gases are present in-frame; for ambient-temperature smoke the thermal channel carries near-zero incremental information, and models trained with fusion degrade on cool smoke relative to visible-only models because they learned to rely on heat.
falsifiable_prediction: Stratifying paired thermal-visible smoke data by measured smoke temperature contrast will show fusion benefit shrinking to zero (or negative) in the low-contrast stratum; a fusion model's attention or ablation analysis will show thermal reliance predicting its cool-smoke failures.
why_important: Procurement decisions for wildfire and industrial monitoring are being made on the assumption that thermal helps with smoke; a regime-dependent null would redirect budgets toward the sensors that actually address the failure cases.
why_possibly_novel: Fusion papers report average gains; a temperature-contrast-stratified audit with a learned-overreliance test appears missing (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Capture or assemble paired data spanning hot and cool smoke (fog machines are ambient; controlled burns are hot), train/evaluate fusion vs visible-only under stratification.
main_risk: Public paired datasets may lack cool-smoke coverage entirely, requiring new captures and limiting the audit's initial scope.
community_default_belief: Adding thermal sensing reliably improves smoke detection and segmentation.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The thermal channel senses temperature, not particulates; the correlation between the two is a property of the dataset's fire-heavy composition, not of smoke.
fastest_falsification: Fusion-vs-visible comparison on ambient fog-machine footage with a thermal camera.

one_line: A two-band visible/near-infrared contrast ratio estimates scattering particle size, physically separating fine smoke from coarse fog and dust where RGB texture models fail.
problem: Smoke-vs-fog-vs-dust confusion is a leading false-alarm source; particle-size differences between these media produce wavelength-dependent scattering that RGB pipelines cannot resolve.
core_hypothesis: The ratio of local contrast attenuation between a visible band and a near-infrared band is a monotone proxy for scattering particle size in the relevant regimes, so a two-band sensor with a per-region ratio feature separates fine combustion smoke from coarse water fog and mineral dust with accuracy unreachable by single-band texture analysis.
falsifiable_prediction: Controlled chamber measurements with characterized aerosols will show the ratio ordering media by particle size as scattering theory predicts; a two-band field prototype will discriminate smoke from fog banks and dust plumes at ranges where RGB models are near chance.
why_important: A physically grounded discriminator for the hardest confusion class would directly cut wildfire-system false alarms and define a minimal sensing requirement instead of an ever-growing data requirement.
why_possibly_novel: Multi-spectral aerosol characterization is established in atmospheric science instrumentation; porting it as a two-band feature for camera-based media segmentation appears rare (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Aerosol-chamber captures across media with a filter-wheel camera, ratio-feature separation analysis, then a small outdoor validation against co-located reference observations.
main_risk: Background reflectance varies spectrally too, contaminating the ratio; the feature likely needs background-normalization machinery that could erode its simplicity.
community_default_belief: Media confusion will be solved in software with more diverse RGB training data.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The discriminating variable (particle size) is spectrally encoded and RGB bands are too close together to read it; no amount of RGB data adds the missing measurement.
fastest_falsification: Chamber ratio measurements across two aerosol types with a filter-wheel camera.

one_line: Depth-sensor dropout patterns are material signatures: glass, mirrors, and smoke corrupt active depth in distinguishable ways, providing free training labels from any RGB-D stream.
problem: Active depth sensors fail on transparent and volumetric media, and these failures are discarded as missing data rather than read as a material-classification channel.
core_hypothesis: The joint statistics of depth invalidity, depth-behind-surface readings, and intensity dropouts form clusster-separable signatures for glass (far-surface or specular dropout), mirrors (geometry-inconsistent phantom depth), and dense smoke (range-dependent attenuation), so an unsupervised clustering of failure patterns yields material pseudo-labels that can bootstrap segmentation training with zero human annotation.
falsifiable_prediction: On RGB-D captures containing known glass/mirror/media regions, failure-pattern clusters will align with material ground truth at high purity; a segmenter distilled from these pseudo-labels will approach weakly supervised baselines on public transparent-object data.
why_important: Billions of RGB-D frames from robots and phones contain this free signal; converting sensor failure into supervision would unlock material-aware training at otherwise impossible scale.
why_possibly_novel: Depth invalidity is used heuristically to find glass in robotics; a systematic multi-material signature taxonomy with distillation-quality validation appears unassembled (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Curate RGB-D scenes with the three material classes, cluster failure statistics, measure cluster-material purity, distill and evaluate a small segmenter.
main_risk: Sensor-model dependence: signatures may differ across structured-light, stereo, and time-of-flight devices, fragmenting the taxonomy into per-hardware variants.
community_default_belief: Depth dropout is noise to be inpainted or masked out before learning.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The dropout is caused by the material's optical properties, making it a measurement of exactly the property segmentation wants to recover.
fastest_falsification: Cluster-purity analysis on a handful of scenes per material with one sensor.

one_line: Audio crackle can weakly supervise flame segmentation via sound-source localization, but the load-bearing question is whether audio localization is spatially sharp enough to teach pixels anything.
problem: Fire emits distinctive broadband crackle; audio-visual learning could supply free flame labels, yet the spatial resolution of audio localization versus the spatial precision segmentation needs has never been confronted for this task.
core_hypothesis: Audio-visual correspondence learning on fire videos yields spatial supervision at a characterizable (coarse) resolution, and this coarse supervision is sufficient to train flame localization to within a bounded factor of pixel-supervised models, because flame appearance is locally distinctive once a rough region is pinned.
falsifiable_prediction: Audio-derived attention maps on multichannel fire recordings will localize flames to region-level accuracy; models trained only on audio-anchored pseudo-labels will reach a substantial fraction of pixel-supervised performance, with the gap concentrated in silent fire types (smoldering), mapping the method's envelope.
why_important: Free supervision from a modality that cameras already often record would enlarge fire training data by orders of magnitude without annotation cost, and the envelope result clarifies which fire regimes remain annotation-dependent.
why_possibly_novel: Audio-visual localization is established for speakers and instruments; a quantified sufficiency analysis for fire segmentation supervision appears absent (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble fire videos with usable audio, train audio-visual correspondence, measure localization sharpness, distill and compare against pixel-supervised baselines.
main_risk: Wind and ambient noise dominate many outdoor recordings; the usable-audio fraction of wild fire footage may be too small to matter.
community_default_belief: Segmentation supervision must come from human masks or visual pseudo-labels; audio is a detection modality at best.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Supervision only needs to be spatially informative, not pixel-precise, when the target's local appearance is distinctive; fire may sit exactly in that regime.
fastest_falsification: Localization-sharpness measurement of audio attention on a few dozen crackling-fire clips.

one_line: Flash/no-flash differencing is a near-direct nighttime smoke densitometer: backscatter from the flash illuminates near-camera media while barely changing the background.
problem: Night smoke detection is hard for passive cameras, yet a controllable illuminant (flash, IR illuminator) creates a differential measurement that isolates scattering media by their backscatter; this measurement model is unformalized for segmentation.
core_hypothesis: The difference image between flash and no-flash frames is approximately proportional to near-field scattering density along each ray (given background distance), so thresholding or regressing on flash differentials yields nighttime smoke masks and relative density maps with quality unreachable by passive night imaging, degrading predictably with smoke-to-camera distance.
falsifiable_prediction: Controlled night captures with metered fog will show flash-differential magnitude tracking measured density; segmentation from differentials will beat passive low-light models sharply at near range and lose to them beyond a characterizable distance where flash falloff dominates.
why_important: Indoor and vehicle-mounted night smoke detection (tunnels, warehouses) operates exactly in the near-field regime; a physics-first differential channel offers reliability that low-light learning has struggled to deliver.
why_possibly_novel: Flash/no-flash pairs are classic in computational photography for denoising; their use as a participating-media densitometer for segmentation appears unexplored (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Night fog-machine sessions with synchronized flash alternation, densitometer readings, differential-based segmentation vs passive baselines across distances.
main_risk: Moving scenes between paired frames create differential artifacts; the method may need high-rate alternation or optical synchronization to stay clean.
community_default_belief: Night smoke perception is a low-light enhancement problem for passive imagery.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Active differential imaging changes the information content, not just the SNR; the backscatter term contains density directly, which no enhancement of passive frames can recover.
fastest_falsification: Differential-vs-density curve from one night session with metered fog.

one_line: Rolling-shutter row-phase artifacts encode flame temporal dynamics within single frames, turning a sensor defect into a static-image flame-vs-flame-colored-object discriminator.
problem: Single-image fire detection cannot use flicker, its most distinctive temporal cue; rolling-shutter cameras, however, sample different image rows at different times, embedding temporal structure inside each frame unnoticed.
core_hypothesis: Flames imaged by rolling-shutter sensors exhibit row-wise intensity phase patterns (horizontal banding statistics) reflecting their rapid luminance dynamics, absent in static flame-colored objects (sunsets, orange fabrics, lamps), and a row-spectrum feature detects this within single frames at useful accuracy.
falsifiable_prediction: Row-direction spectral analysis of single frames will separate real flames from flame-colored static distractors well above chance on rolling-shutter footage, will fail on global-shutter footage of the same scenes (the causal control), and the effect will scale with readout time as the mechanism predicts.
why_important: A single-frame dynamic cue would harden image-based fire detectors against their canonical false positives without requiring video, relevant for photo-based alerting and forensics.
why_possibly_novel: Rolling shutter is exploited to measure light flicker and propeller speeds; its use for flame discrimination in static imagery appears unproposed (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Capture flames and matched distractors with rolling- and global-shutter cameras, extract row-spectral features, run the separation and the shutter-type causal control.
main_risk: The effect size at typical readout speeds and flame distances may be tiny, drowned by texture; the chamber-style close-range result may not survive real distances.
community_default_belief: Single images fundamentally cannot carry flicker information; temporal fire cues require video.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Rolling-shutter frames are not instantaneous samples but row-time-multiplexed recordings; the temporal axis is folded into the spatial one and remains partially recoverable.
fastest_falsification: Row-spectrum separation test on close-range flame vs distractor stills from one rolling-shutter phone.

one_line: Fire segmenters are largely saturated-warm-color detectors: a color-reliance index computed via hue-rotation counterfactuals predicts their false positives and their grayscale collapse.
problem: Fire has strong shape, texture, and glow cues besides color, but training data makes color overwhelmingly predictive; the degree of color shortcut reliance has not been quantified per model.
core_hypothesis: Public fire segmenters' outputs are dominated by a low-dimensional color subspace: hue-rotating fire regions toward blue suppresses detection almost entirely, hue-rotating distractors toward orange induces confident false masks, and a scalar color-reliance index derived from these counterfactuals predicts each model's real-world false-positive rate on sunsets, foliage, and clothing.
falsifiable_prediction: Counterfactual hue manipulations will move model outputs by large factors while shape/texture manipulations of matched magnitude barely move them; the derived index will rank models by distractor false-alarm rate with high correlation.
why_important: Gas and alcohol fires burn blue and are missed catastrophically if color is the load-bearing feature; the index also gives buyers a one-number audit of a detector's shortcut exposure.
why_possibly_novel: Color shortcut concerns are folklore; a standardized counterfactual index validated as a predictor of deployment false alarms appears unbuilt for fire models (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement hue-rotation and texture-scramble counterfactuals, compute indices for public checkpoints, correlate with false-alarm rates on a distractor suite.
main_risk: Naive hue rotation produces off-manifold images; needs photorealistic recoloring or physical blue-flame footage to avoid measuring off-distribution weirdness instead of shortcut reliance.
community_default_belief: Modern segmenters integrate shape, texture, and context; color is one cue among many.
why_that_may_be_wrong: When one cue is near-perfectly predictive in training data, gradient descent has no incentive to maintain redundant cues; the resulting reliance is invisible until the cue breaks.
fastest_falsification: Hue-rotation counterfactuals on one checkpoint across a dozen fire images.

one_line: Smoke segmenters are partly skyline detectors: performance collapses for smoke below the horizon line because datasets overwhelmingly show plumes against sky.
problem: Wildfire imagery is dominated by plumes rising above terrain into sky; smoke seen against ground, vegetation, or buildings (valley fires, viewed from above) is rare in training data, creating a suspected but unmeasured positional shortcut.
core_hypothesis: Model recall for physically identical smoke is substantially lower when the plume is imaged against terrain backgrounds than against sky, beyond what background contrast differences explain, because models learned 'gray mass touching skyline' as a proxy; drone-view (top-down) smoke suffers most.
falsifiable_prediction: Controlled composites and real matched pairs (same smoke, sky vs terrain backing) will show a recall gap persisting after equalizing local contrast; error maps will show misses clustering below the estimated horizon; view-angle stratification of existing datasets will reproduce the effect on real data.
why_important: Valley fires and aerial firefighting views are high-stakes cases; a skyline shortcut means the system fails precisely off the photogenic distribution, and the fix (terrain-backed training data) is concrete.
why_possibly_novel: Context bias is generic knowledge; isolating the horizon/skyline shortcut with contrast-controlled counterfactuals for smoke appears specific and undone (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build contrast-matched sky/terrain smoke pairs (compositing plus fog-machine captures against hillsides), evaluate public models, decompose the recall gap into contrast vs position components.
main_risk: Sky backgrounds genuinely offer higher physical contrast for thin smoke, so the decomposition must be careful not to over-attribute physics to shortcut.
community_default_belief: Smoke recall differences across scenes reflect visibility physics, not learned positional priors.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Training distributions concentrate plumes at skylines, and networks demonstrably absorb positional statistics; physics and prior are confounded until someone controls for contrast.
fastest_falsification: Contrast-matched composite pairs through one public model.

one_line: Tight-cropping collapses smoke recognition far more than solid-object recognition, revealing that models possess almost no intrinsic appearance model of the medium itself.
problem: It is unknown how much of smoke-segmentation competence resides in the medium's own appearance versus surrounding scene evidence; the standard context-ablation methodology has not been applied comparatively.
core_hypothesis: Removing context by tight cropping (or context scrambling) degrades smoke segmentation accuracy by a much larger fraction than it degrades solid-object segmentation, demonstrating that current models encode 'scenes where smoke happens' rather than 'what smoke looks like', with implications for their behavior in novel scene types.
falsifiable_prediction: The context-dependence ratio (accuracy drop under crop, normalized) will be several-fold higher for smoke than for a matched solid-object suite across multiple architectures; cross-scene-type generalization failures will correlate with each model's context-dependence ratio.
why_important: If media competence is mostly contextual, then dataset diversity in scene types (not smoke instances) is the binding constraint, inverting current data-collection priorities.
why_possibly_novel: Context ablation is a standard tool; the comparative quantification for media vs solids and its use as a generalization predictor appears missing (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run crop/scramble ablations over smoke and solid datasets on public models, compute dependence ratios, correlate with cross-dataset transfer scores.
main_risk: Cropping alters resolution and object-scale statistics simultaneously; needs scale-matched controls to attribute the drop to context loss.
community_default_belief: Segmenters primarily recognize target appearance, with context as a helpful auxiliary signal.
why_that_may_be_wrong: For low-distinctiveness targets like gray translucent volumes, context may be the primary signal and appearance the auxiliary one, a silent inversion of the assumed architecture of the learned solution.
fastest_falsification: Dependence-ratio computation for one smoke and one solid dataset on one model.

one_line: Video compression destroys smoke evidence before it destroys solid-object evidence: deployed CCTV bitrates may sit past a cliff where smoke segmentation has silently collapsed.
problem: Smoke's signal lives in low-contrast gradients and subtle temporal decorrelation, exactly what lossy codecs remove first; benchmarks use high-quality video, deployments use starved encoders, and the gap is uncharacterized.
core_hypothesis: Segmentation accuracy versus bitrate curves are qualitatively different for smoke (steep collapse below a threshold bitrate, driven by gradient quantization and temporal smoothing) than for solid objects (graceful degradation), and common surveillance encoder settings fall below the smoke cliff.
falsifiable_prediction: Re-encoding evaluation sets across bitrates will show the differential collapse; the collapse point will track codec quantization parameters affecting low-contrast blocks; models fine-tuned on compressed data will shift but not remove the cliff, because the information (not the features) is gone.
why_important: If true, many deployed smoke-detection systems are certified on data their cameras never produce, a systemic safety blind spot with a measurable boundary that operators could fix in encoder configuration.
why_possibly_novel: Compression robustness studies exist for detection; the media-specific cliff hypothesis tied to codec low-contrast behavior, plus the encoder-configuration remedy, appears unexamined (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Bitrate-sweep re-encoding of smoke and solid benchmarks, accuracy curves for public models, fine-tuning control, comparison of cliff location against surveyed CCTV encoder defaults.
main_risk: Codec implementations differ; the cliff may be encoder-specific, requiring a survey across common hardware encoders for the deployment claim.
community_default_belief: Compression robustness is a uniform, second-order concern handled by data augmentation.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Codecs are perceptual optimizers that explicitly discard what smoke is made of (low-saliency low-contrast change); augmentation cannot restore discarded bits.
fastest_falsification: Accuracy-vs-bitrate curves on one smoke set and one solid set with one model.

one_line: Fire context primes smoke hallucination: models exposed to any fire-colored region label nearby fog and haze as smoke, a contextual induction effect measurable with composite scenes.
problem: Fog co-occurring with fire cues (vehicle lights, orange reflections, burnt terrain) is the operationally critical discrimination case, but datasets contain few such combinations and models' contextual coupling between fire and smoke channels is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: The presence of fire-typical evidence anywhere in the frame raises smoke false-positive rates on unrelated fog/haze regions multiplicatively (not additively), because models learned a scene-level joint prior rather than independent per-region evidence integration; the coupling strength can be measured by factorial composites.
falsifiable_prediction: A factorial design (fog present/absent x fire-cue present/absent, spatially disjoint) will show super-additive smoke false positives in the fog+fire-cue cell across public models; ablating scene-level pathways (e.g. restricting receptive fields) will reduce the coupling at some cost to true detection.
why_important: Emergency scenes are saturated with fire cues; a multiplicative hallucination effect means the systems are least reliable exactly during incidents, when false situation reports are most damaging.
why_possibly_novel: Co-occurrence bias is well known; measuring cross-region multiplicative coupling with factorial composites for the fire-smoke pair appears new (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build the factorial composite set from real fog footage and inserted fire cues, run public models, fit additive vs multiplicative interaction models to false-positive rates.
main_risk: Compositing artifacts may themselves drive responses; a real-capture subset (fog scenes with actual distant flames) is needed for confirmation.
community_default_belief: False positives are per-region appearance errors; scene context only helps by adding evidence.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Joint training on correlated scenes teaches a scene-level prior that overrides local evidence; context then manufactures detections rather than refining them.
fastest_falsification: The 2x2 composite grid through one model.

one_line: Transparent-object models are rim detectors: inpainting the frame/rim of glassware collapses segmentation, exposing that the interior 'transparency understanding' is interpolation between detected edges.
problem: Glass masks look impressively complete, but whether interiors are perceived or merely interpolated from rims and frames has not been causally tested.
core_hypothesis: Removing rim evidence (inpainting rims, imaging rimless vessels, framing glass so edges are out of view) collapses interior segmentation accuracy disproportionately, showing that current models detect boundary artifacts and fill inward, with near-zero reliance on interior refraction or reflection cues.
falsifiable_prediction: Rim-inpainted counterfactuals will reduce interior mask accuracy by a large factor while equally sized non-rim occlusions barely matter; rimless laboratory glassware and edge-cropped compositions will show the same collapse on real data; models' saliency will concentrate on rims at rates far exceeding rim area.
why_important: Robotic manipulation reaches for glass interiors, not rims; interpolation-based masks give false confidence about exactly the region grippers and liquid-level estimators need.
why_possibly_novel: Edge reliance is suspected in the subfield; the causal inpainting design with matched-size occlusion controls and the rimless-vessel real-data confirmation appears unexecuted (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct rim-inpainted and control-occluded versions of glass benchmark images, evaluate public models, then verify on photographed rimless vessels.
main_risk: Inpainting quality could leak cues; needs multiple inpainting methods and the real rimless subset as the decisive condition.
community_default_belief: Modern glass segmenters integrate reflection, distortion, and boundary cues over the whole object.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Rims are the only high-SNR, spatially reliable cue in most training images; optimization plausibly concentrated all effective capacity there, leaving interior cues unlearned.
fastest_falsification: Rim-inpainting ablation on one model over a few dozen images.

one_line: Steam, smoke, clouds, spray, and fog occupy one undifferentiated 'white volumetric stuff' region in current models' feature space, and representational geometry predicts which confusions are fixable by fine-tuning versus structural.
problem: Deployment requires distinguishing white-media classes, yet the internal representational structure that determines whether these distinctions are learnable-by-fine-tuning has never been mapped.
core_hypothesis: Feature-space analysis (probing, representational similarity) of standard backbones will show white-media classes nearly collinear/overlapping relative to solid-class separations; the degree of overlap per class pair predicts fine-tuning sample efficiency for that discrimination, separating 'latent but unread' distinctions from 'never encoded' ones.
falsifiable_prediction: Linear separability of white-media pairs in frozen features will be dramatically lower than for solid pairs; fine-tuning learning curves per pair will rank-correlate with frozen-feature separability; pairs at chance separability will remain data-hungry regardless of head design, confirming the structural diagnosis.
why_important: Tells practitioners whether to spend on labels (if latent) or on new sensing/inputs (if never encoded) per confusion pair, replacing blind data collection with a measurement-driven decision.
why_possibly_novel: Representational analyses target semantic categories; applying separability-predicts-finetunability logic to the white-media family appears new (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble labeled patches per class, run probing and similarity analyses on several frozen backbones, then fine-tuning curves per pair, test the predicted correlation.
main_risk: Patch-level labels for wispy media are noisy; class overlap measured may partly reflect label contamination rather than representation.
community_default_belief: Any distinction present in labels can be fine-tuned into a strong backbone given moderate data.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Self-supervised and classification pretraining had no pressure to separate white volumetric media; some distinctions may be absent from the representation, making fine-tuning data requirements explode.
fastest_falsification: Frozen-feature separability matrix for the five classes on one backbone.

one_line: Night-fire masks largely trace the camera's glare and bloom, not the fire: models segment the sensor's point-spread function, and mask area is predictable from exposure settings alone.
problem: Night fire imagery is dominated by blooming, veiling glare, and saturation halos generated by optics and sensor overload; what fraction of 'fire masks' consists of these artifacts is unknown.
core_hypothesis: For night scenes, a large fraction of predicted fire-mask area lies in bloom/glare regions rather than combustion regions, and mask area scales with exposure and aperture as the optical point-spread model predicts, meaning night-fire benchmark scores substantially measure reproduction of camera artifacts.
falsifiable_prediction: Bracketed night captures will show predicted mask area tracking exposure as glare physics dictates; HDR reconstruction or anti-glare optics will shrink masks toward combustion regions, and models will disagree with the corrected imagery in proportion to their artifact reliance; fire-size estimates derived from masks will be biased upward at night by a predictable factor.
why_important: Downstream consumers use mask area for fire-size and spread estimation; artifact-inflated masks corrupt those estimates systematically at night, when response decisions are hardest.
why_possibly_novel: Glare is a known photographic phenomenon; quantifying its share of night-fire segmentation output and the exposure-scaling law appears undone (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Night bracketed captures of controlled fires with and without anti-glare measures, run public models, decompose mask area into combustion-consistent and glare-consistent components.
main_risk: Separating true flame from glare in ground truth requires careful physical instrumentation (e.g. thermal reference), without which the decomposition is circular.
community_default_belief: Night fire is the easy case: fire is bright, models find it, high scores reflect competence.
