why_that_may_be_wrong: Brightness makes detection easy while making delineation meaningless; the visible extent at night is mostly an instrument response, so high delineation scores measure artifact mimicry.
fastest_falsification: Mask-area vs exposure curve for one model on one bracketed night sequence.

one_line: Detection latency on growing plumes is the hidden casualty of dataset curation: models trained on photogenic developed plumes activate far later on incipient smoke than their benchmark scores imply.
problem: Datasets curate images where smoke is clearly visible, truncating the early phase of plume development; the resulting latency distribution of detectors on full ignition-to-plume timelines is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: On continuous recordings spanning ignition to developed plume, current models' first-detection times cluster long after human observers' detection times, and the lag correlates with the training set's plume-size distribution: the model has learned what curated smoke looks like, which is definitionally not what early smoke looks like.
falsifiable_prediction: Timeline evaluations on controlled ignitions will show a systematic model-vs-human latency gap; retraining with timeline-sampled (uncurated) data will reduce latency substantially at fixed false-alarm rate, quantifying the curation penalty; frame-level benchmark scores will fail to predict latency ranking across models.
why_important: Latency is the actual objective of early-warning systems; if benchmarks do not predict it, the field is optimizing a proxy that diverges from the mission on the axis that matters most.
why_possibly_novel: Latency metrics exist in event detection; connecting curation-induced distribution truncation to segmentation-model latency with a controlled ignition protocol appears new (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Record controlled ignition timelines, measure model and human first-detection distributions, retrain with timeline sampling, compare latency and benchmark-score orderings.
main_risk: Controlled ignitions constrain fuel and scale diversity; wild validation would need opportunistic full recordings, which are rare.
community_default_belief: Better frame-level segmentation scores translate to earlier detection in deployment.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Frame-level scores average over the curated visibility distribution; latency depends on the truncated tail that curation removed from both training and evaluation.
fastest_falsification: Latency-vs-benchmark-rank comparison for three models on a handful of ignition timelines.

one_line: A taxonomy of 'natural adversarials' for media segmentation (birch trunks, waterfalls, sunbeams, dust devils, contrails) can explain the majority of field false positives with a small closed list.
problem: False positives in deployed smoke/fire systems are treated as a long tail, but practitioners repeatedly mention the same scene types; whether the tail is actually short has never been tested.
core_hypothesis: Field false positives concentrate heavily on a small enumerable set of physically smoke-like or fire-like natural phenomena, such that a taxonomy of under twenty categories covers the large majority of false-positive volume, making targeted negative curation vastly more efficient than generic data scaling.
falsifiable_prediction: Clustering false positives from deployed-system logs (or from public models run over large unlabeled outdoor video corpora) will yield a category histogram with strong head concentration; negative fine-tuning on only the head categories will remove most false-positive volume while generic negatives of equal count remove far less.
why_important: Converts false-alarm reduction from an open-ended data problem into a bounded curation checklist, with direct cost implications for system operators.
why_possibly_novel: Hard-negative mining is standard; the empirical claim that the media-distractor distribution has a short head, validated by targeted-vs-generic curation efficiency, appears untested (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run public models over diverse outdoor video corpora, cluster and hand-categorize false positives, measure head concentration, run the targeted-vs-generic fine-tuning comparison.
main_risk: The head may be camera-placement-dependent (forest lookouts vs urban CCTV), making the taxonomy deployment-specific and the universal claim false in an instructive way.
community_default_belief: False positives form an unbounded long tail addressable only by scale and continual learning.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The physics of looking-like-smoke is restrictive (gray, translucent, textured motion); few natural phenomena satisfy it, so the distractor space may be intrinsically small.
fastest_falsification: False-positive clustering from one model over one large corpus.

one_line: Predicting log-transmittance (optical depth) instead of masks makes smoke composition additive, enabling extrapolation to densities never seen in training.
problem: Mask and alpha output spaces saturate: dense smoke and very dense smoke look identical in labels, so models cannot represent 'more than opaque', and overlapping plumes have no compositional semantics.
core_hypothesis: Training media models to regress log-transmittance makes overlapping smoke linear in the output space (optical depths add along rays), so models trained only on single-plume scenes will predict two-plume overlaps correctly (additivity generalization) and extrapolate beyond the training density range, which alpha- and mask-space models will fail.
falsifiable_prediction: On rendered and controlled real scenes, log-space models will predict overlap regions with low error despite never seeing overlaps in training, while alpha-space equivalents will underestimate systematically; extrapolation error beyond training density will grow much slower in log space.
why_important: Compositional generalization from cheap single-source data to complex multi-source scenes would slash data requirements for industrial and wildfire settings where dense multi-plume scenes are dangerous to stage.
why_possibly_novel: Log-domain processing is standard in tomography and atmospheric optics; testing additivity generalization as a learning-theoretic benefit for media segmentation output spaces appears new (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Render single-plume training and multi-plume test sets with ground-truth optical depth, train matched models in mask/alpha/log spaces, compare overlap and extrapolation errors; validate on dual fog-machine captures.
main_risk: Log-space targets amplify supervision noise in near-transparent regions; loss weighting choices may drive the comparison more than the representation.
community_default_belief: Output-space choice among mask, alpha, and density variants is a minor implementation detail.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Output spaces define which generalizations are linear and hence learnable from limited data; for participating media, physics says only log-transmittance composes additively.
fastest_falsification: Overlap-additivity test on rendered data with small models in two output spaces.

one_line: Predicting a monotone stack of nested iso-density contours turns one arbitrary annotation threshold into a family, making threshold choice explicit and letting one model serve every application's strictness.
problem: Different applications need different smoke thresholds (early warning wants sensitivity, compositing wants cores), but each dataset bakes in one threshold and each model serves only that one.
core_hypothesis: A model constrained to output nested mask families (monotone level sets) trained on mixed-threshold data disentangles 'where the density gradient lies' from 'where one annotator cut it', producing per-level accuracy on held-out strictness levels it never saw labeled, which single-threshold models cannot do.
falsifiable_prediction: Trained on strict-only and loose-only labels from disjoint image sets, the level-set model will predict intermediate-strictness annotations of a third set better than interpolation between two single-threshold models; violations of nesting in unconstrained models will correlate with their cross-threshold errors.
why_important: Decouples dataset threshold politics from model capability and provides a single deployable artifact for heterogeneous consumers, directly addressing the annotator-threshold pathology (C-001) at the representation level.
why_possibly_novel: Ordinal/level-set structure exists in other domains; its use to absorb annotation-threshold heterogeneity in media segmentation appears unexplored (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Dual-strictness annotation (reusing the C-001 protocol), train level-set and baseline models, evaluate on a held-out intermediate-strictness annotation set.
main_risk: The monotonicity constraint may fight genuine multi-modal ambiguity (disconnected wisps appearing before cores under some orderings), requiring topology-aware relaxations.
community_default_belief: A segmentation model should output the mask matching its training labels; multi-threshold needs are handled by post-hoc logit thresholding.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Logits of a single-threshold model are calibrated to one label function and interpolate unreliably; explicit ordinal structure is trained, not assumed.
fastest_falsification: Cross-threshold prediction test with small models on one dual-annotated dataset.

one_line: The correct target for ambiguous boundaries is a boundary distribution, not a boundary: models should be scored by the likelihood they assign to the population of plausible annotations.
problem: All standard pipelines output one boundary and are scored against one reference, though the annotation process for media demonstrably produces a distribution; the modeling and evaluation mismatch compounds.
core_hypothesis: Modeling the mask as a distribution (a generative model over plausible masks conditioned on the image) and evaluating by held-out multi-annotator likelihood will rank models differently than point-mask metrics, and distribution-trained models will transfer better across annotation protocols because they capture the ambiguity structure rather than one protocol's realization.
falsifiable_prediction: On multi-annotator media data, likelihood-based ranking will diverge from IoU ranking; distribution-trained models will lose less when evaluated against a new annotator pool than point-trained models, with the retained advantage concentrated in high-ambiguity regions.
why_important: Aligns the learning target with the actual data-generating process for the entire class of boundary-undefined objects, potentially resolving the cross-protocol fragility documented in this territory.
why_possibly_novel: Stochastic segmentation networks exist in medical imaging; the cross-protocol transfer claim as the decisive advantage for volumetric media appears untested (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train point and distributional models on a multi-annotator smoke set, evaluate likelihood and IoU rankings, run the new-annotator-pool transfer test.
main_risk: Multi-annotator media data at scale barely exists; the experiment requires building it, which is the real cost of the idea.
community_default_belief: One good mask per image is the correct output; ambiguity is handled by confidence maps if at all.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Confidence maps are per-pixel marginals that cannot represent correlated boundary uncertainty (whole wisps present or absent together), which is the dominant ambiguity structure in media.
fastest_falsification: Marginal-vs-joint ambiguity check: test whether annotator disagreement is spatially correlated beyond per-pixel independence on any multi-annotator subset.

one_line: Decomposing glass into reflection layer, transmission layer, and distortion field makes segmentation a byproduct, and synthetic-only training of the decomposition may transfer better than real-supervised direct masking.
problem: Direct mask supervision for glass entangles all optical phenomena into one binary decision, learning dataset-specific mixtures; the physically factored representation might be the transferable one, but the transfer comparison has never been run.
core_hypothesis: A model trained (on synthetic data where all layers are known) to decompose images into reflection, transmission, and refraction-distortion components learns physics-anchored features that transfer to real glass segmentation with less real data than direct mask models need, because the decomposition is domain-general while mask boundaries are dataset-specific.
falsifiable_prediction: In a transfer protocol (synthetic pretraining, few-shot real adaptation), the decomposition model will dominate direct-mask synthetic pretraining at all few-shot sizes; its advantage will be largest on optical-phenomenon-rich glass (curved, coated) and smallest on flat framed panes where masks are edge-driven.
why_important: Synthetic data for glass is unlimited and perfectly labeled at the physics level; if physics-factored pretraining is the right way to spend it, the field's synthetic pipelines need retargeting from masks to layers.
why_possibly_novel: Reflection separation and intrinsic decomposition are established tasks; using them as the pretraining objective specifically to win the few-shot transfer comparison for glass segmentation appears untested (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build matched synthetic pretraining runs (layers vs masks), few-shot adapt both on real glass data, compare adaptation curves and stratify by glass type.
main_risk: Renderer realism for coated/dirty real glass may bound both approaches equally, muting the comparison; needs a renderer-quality sweep to check.
community_default_belief: The shortest path to a segmentation model is supervising the segmentation output directly.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Direct supervision of an entangled decision learns the dataset's phenomenon mixture; supervising the physical factors learns the invariants the decision should be computed from.
fastest_falsification: Few-shot transfer comparison at a single small shot count.

one_line: Media and their distractors separate in a joint spatial-temporal frequency representation: smoke occupies a characteristic low-spatial/broadband-temporal cell that a spectrally factored model can exploit and standard architectures blur away.
problem: Convolutional and attention architectures mix frequency content indiscriminately; if media are spectrally localized in a joint space, generic mixing may destroy separability that a factored representation preserves.
core_hypothesis: In a joint spatial-frequency x temporal-frequency decomposition of video, smoke concentrates in an identifiable region (low spatial frequencies with broadband temporal decorrelation) distinct from solid textures, vegetation, and camera noise; an architecture that processes this decomposition explicitly achieves equal accuracy to standard models at a large parameter reduction, and degrades more gracefully under domain shift.
falsifiable_prediction: Energy-distribution measurements across labeled classes will confirm the spectral localization; the factored model will match standard baselines at a fraction of parameters on smoke tasks and lose that advantage on solid-object tasks, tying the benefit to the media's spectral structure rather than general efficiency.
why_important: A validated spectral characterization gives the field a compact, interpretable prior for the whole media family, informing architecture, compression settings, and sensor design simultaneously.
why_possibly_novel: Spatio-temporal filtering is classical; a quantitative joint-spectral atlas of media vs distractors driving an architecture-efficiency claim appears absent (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute joint spectra per class over labeled video corpora, verify localization, build the factored model, run the matched-accuracy parameter comparison.
main_risk: Spectral localization may vary with imaging distance and wind, smearing the atlas and reducing the factored model's edge to nothing.
community_default_belief: End-to-end learned features subsume any hand-designed spectral structure; explicit decompositions add nothing.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Subsumption assumes sufficient data along all axes; media data is scarce, and a correct prior substitutes for exactly the data the field does not have.
fastest_falsification: Joint-spectra measurement across classes on existing labeled videos.

one_line: Turbulent internal motion is a monocular depth cue inside plumes: smoke's 3D structure is partially recoverable from single-camera video, making 2D segmentation a projection of a solvable 3D problem.
problem: Plume perception is treated as irreducibly 2D from monocular video, yet internal turbulent features at different depths move with different image velocities (parallax and size-speed statistics), an untapped structure-from-motion signal for volumes.
core_hypothesis: The statistics of feature motion within a smoke region (velocity dispersion, occlusion ordering of transient features) constrain relative depth layering inside the plume well enough that a monocular video model can recover coarse 3D density structure, verifiable against multi-view reconstruction, and 3D-aware training improves 2D segmentation consistency across views for free.
falsifiable_prediction: Monocular predictions of plume depth layering will agree with two-camera reconstructions well above chance; models with the 3D auxiliary objective will show measurably higher cross-view 2D mask consistency (idea C-005's metric) than 2D-only models of equal capacity.
why_important: Coarse plume 3D from ubiquitous single cameras would upgrade smoke monitoring from detection to volumetric estimation (spread direction, volume growth) without new hardware.
why_possibly_novel: Structure-from-motion for rigid scenes is mature; exploiting turbulence statistics as a depth cue inside participating media appears speculative and unexplored (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Two-camera fog-machine captures for ground truth, train monocular depth-layering predictors on one view, validate against reconstruction, then run the cross-view-consistency comparison.
main_risk: Turbulent feature correspondence may be too short-lived for reliable motion estimation, making the signal practically inaccessible even if theoretically present.
community_default_belief: Monocular video of homogeneous media carries no usable depth information; volumetric estimates require multi-view or active sensing.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Turbulence continuously generates trackable transient texture throughout the volume; the medium is not homogeneous at the timescales that matter, and each transient feature is a parallax probe.
fastest_falsification: Measure whether tracked transient features' velocities stratify consistently with two-camera depth on a single capture.

one_line: Per-pixel transparent-surface counting (0/1/2+ layers) is a learnable output space that fixes the self-overlap failures binary glass masks cannot even express.
problem: Binary glass masks collapse layered transparency into one bit; scenes with nested glass (display cases, double glazing, stacked cookware) are unrepresentable, and models trained on the collapsed space behave incoherently there.
core_hypothesis: Reframing glass segmentation as ordinal layer counting is learnable with modest synthetic supervision, transfers to real layered scenes, and as a side effect improves ordinary single-layer mask accuracy because the counting objective forces the model to localize each optical interface rather than a blurred union.
falsifiable_prediction: A counting-head model trained on synthetic layered scenes plus existing single-layer real data will beat binary models on constructed real layered test scenes by a wide margin (which is near-guaranteed by expressiveness) and, non-trivially, will also improve single-layer boundary accuracy on standard data at equal capacity.
why_important: Retail, laboratory, and architectural environments are dense with layered transparency; robots and AR systems there currently operate on a representation that cannot describe the scene at all.
why_possibly_novel: Layered representations exist for opaque amodal reasoning; ordinal interface counting for transparency with the single-layer side-benefit claim appears new (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Extend a synthetic pipeline to labeled layer counts, train counting and binary models, evaluate on constructed layered real scenes and standard single-layer benchmarks.
main_risk: Real supervision for layer counts is expensive and human counting reliability beyond two layers is doubtful, capping evaluable depth.
community_default_belief: Binary glass-or-not masks are the appropriate output; layering is a rare corner case not worth representational cost.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Layered transparency is routine indoors (windows behind glasses, cabinets), and the corner-case framing reflects dataset composition rather than the world; expressiveness failures silently corrupt even single-layer predictions near overlaps.
fastest_falsification: Evaluate binary models on constructed layered scenes to document incoherence, then the counting model's margin.

one_line: Media need two masks, not one: 'physically present' vs 'photometrically evident' extents diverge measurably, and supervising their difference resolves annotation contradictions at the source.
problem: Annotation guidelines oscillate between labeling where smoke is and where smoke is visible; the two extents differ (thin smoke present but invisible against matched backgrounds), and forcing one mask makes contradictory labels inevitable.
core_hypothesis: In controlled scenes both extents are separately measurable (presence via physical instrumentation or release geometry, evidence via contrast analysis), their difference region is large for thin media, and jointly supervising both masks yields models whose evidence-mask generalizes across backgrounds while presence-mask calibrates abstention, outperforming single-mask training on each objective separately.
falsifiable_prediction: The presence/evidence divergence region measured in controlled captures will be substantial for thin smoke; dual-headed models will beat single-mask models on background-shifted evaluation (evidence head) and on instrumented presence estimation (presence head), while single-mask models will land incoherently between the two targets.
why_important: Dissolves a genuine ontological contradiction that currently manifests as label noise, cross-dataset inconsistency, and unfixable evaluation disputes for every thin-media dataset.
why_possibly_novel: Visibility vs existence is discussed philosophically in amodal segmentation; operationalizing the split with physical instrumentation for media and testing dual supervision appears new (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Instrumented fog releases over varied backgrounds giving both extents, train dual vs single headed models, evaluate each head on its matched objective.
main_risk: The presence mask is only measurable in controlled setups, so the presence head may not transfer to the wild, limiting the claim to the evidence half plus a calibration story.
community_default_belief: One mask per class per image is the universal, sufficient supervision format for segmentation.
why_that_may_be_wrong: For translucent media the single mask is an unstable compromise between two physically distinct quantities; the instability is the documented annotation chaos, not a fixable guideline problem.
fastest_falsification: Measure the divergence region's size in one controlled capture; if negligible, the dual-mask machinery is unnecessary.

one_line: Amodal completion helps glass but harms smoke: a dissociation experiment that reveals what 'object permanence' means to segmentation models.
problem: Amodal segmentation (predicting occluded extents) is increasingly bolted onto models as a general upgrade, but media have no well-defined occluded extent, and the interaction has never been tested.
core_hypothesis: Adding amodal-completion objectives improves transparent-object segmentation (glass has definite geometry that completion regularizes) while degrading smoke segmentation (completion imposes closed-shape priors on an object with no canonical shape), producing a clean double dissociation that localizes where shape priors help versus hurt in the ambiguous-object family.
falsifiable_prediction: Matched models with and without amodal heads will show opposite-signed effects on glass vs smoke benchmarks; the smoke degradation will concentrate in shape-prior symptoms (over-convexification, wisp deletion) measurable by the topology statistics of C-033.
why_important: The field imports opaque-object machinery into media tasks by default; a demonstrated dissociation would establish that the ambiguous-object family needs task-conditional design, with a concrete diagnostic for when completion is safe.
why_possibly_novel: Amodal work targets opaque occlusion; its interaction with boundary-undefined and transparent classes appears unstudied in either direction (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched pairs (with/without amodal auxiliary) on glass and smoke tasks, compare signed effects and run the shape-prior symptom analysis.
main_risk: Effect sizes may be small relative to training variance, requiring multiple seeds and careful matching to establish the dissociation.
community_default_belief: Amodal reasoning is a universally beneficial ingredient for robust segmentation.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Amodal completion presupposes an object with a definite hidden extent; applying it where the presupposition fails injects a false prior, and media are the canonical presupposition-violating class.
fastest_falsification: Single-seed matched pair on smoke only; a degradation with shape-prior symptoms is the key directional signal.

one_line: Multi-hypothesis mask heads spend their diversity where ambiguity lives: on media they reproduce annotator distributions, on solids they collapse, giving a data-driven ambiguity taxonomy for free.
problem: Diverse-prediction architectures are evaluated on aggregate benchmarks that mix ambiguous and unambiguous content, so where the diversity actually goes and whether it tracks true ambiguity is unknown.
core_hypothesis: Training K-hypothesis segmentation heads on mixed data will yield hypothesis diversity concentrated on media and other boundary-undefined content, quantitatively matching multi-annotator disagreement distributions where those exist, so the trained model's diversity map doubles as an unsupervised ambiguity atlas of any dataset.
falsifiable_prediction: Per-region hypothesis variance will correlate strongly with held-out annotator disagreement on media data and approach zero on solid-object data; applying the trained model to an unlabeled corpus will rank scene types by ambiguity in an order matching independent annotation studies.
why_important: Provides dataset builders an automatic instrument for locating where annotation money buys signal versus noise, and validates (or refutes) multi-hypothesis training as capturing real rather than spurious ambiguity.
why_possibly_novel: Multi-hypothesis segmentation exists; auditing where the diversity allocates and validating it against annotator distributions as an ambiguity measurement tool appears new (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train a K-head model on combined media and solid datasets, correlate hypothesis variance with multi-annotator disagreement on the subset that has it, then run the unlabeled-corpus ranking check.
main_risk: Diversity may instead concentrate on label noise and dataset boundaries (annotation-style differences), measuring supervision inconsistency rather than perceptual ambiguity; distinguishing these requires the multi-annotator anchor.
community_default_belief: Prediction diversity in multi-hypothesis models is an internal mechanism, not a measurement to be read out and trusted.
why_that_may_be_wrong: If the training distribution embeds real ambiguity, a well-calibrated diverse predictor is forced to internalize it, making the readout a legitimate estimator rather than a byproduct.
fastest_falsification: Variance-vs-disagreement correlation on one multi-annotator media subset.

one_line: Scaling web data may make smoke segmentation worse: context shortcuts accumulate faster than appearance signal, so a curated controlled-capture dataset can beat orders of magnitude more scraped data on distractor-heavy tests.
problem: The default assumption is that more data monotonically helps; for classes photographed almost exclusively in stereotyped contexts, scraping may enrich the shortcut, not the concept, and the scaling curve on shortcut-breaking tests has never been drawn.
core_hypothesis: As scraped smoke training data grows, in-distribution benchmark scores rise while performance on context-broken evaluations (atypical-context smoke, typical-context non-smoke) stagnates or declines, whereas a small physically controlled dataset (fog machines across many real scenes) produces better context-broken performance despite far fewer images.
falsifiable_prediction: The scaling curve on context-broken tests will be flat or negative beyond a modest data size for scraped data; the controlled dataset will dominate at equal training cost on those tests while losing slightly on in-distribution benchmarks, and the crossover will be attributable to context-feature reliance measured by ablation.
why_important: Data-scaling is the field's default investment; demonstrating a class of problems where it actively entrenches failure would redirect resources toward capture design for the entire ambiguous-object family.
why_possibly_novel: Shortcut amplification by scale is discussed theoretically; a controlled head-to-head between scraped scale and physical-capture curation for media appears unrun (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched models on nested scraped subsets and on a controlled capture set, evaluate all on shared context-broken and standard tests, draw both scaling curves.
main_risk: Scraped-data cleaning quality is a confound: a critic can always claim better filtering would fix scaling, so the study needs a strong filtered-scraping arm.
community_default_belief: More diverse web data is the most reliable way to improve any recognition task, including smoke.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Web images of smoke are context-selected by the act of photographing smoke; the sampling process is the shortcut generator, and scaling a biased sampler sharpens its bias.
fastest_falsification: Two-point scaling comparison (small vs large scraped subsets) on one context-broken test.

one_line: Downsampling helps smoke segmentation: accuracy versus input resolution is non-monotone for media because high frequencies carry distractor texture but almost no smoke signal.
problem: Higher input resolution is assumed universally beneficial; for a low-spatial-frequency target embedded among high-frequency distractors, the assumption is theoretically doubtful and empirically untested.
core_hypothesis: Smoke segmentation accuracy peaks at a moderate input resolution and declines at native resolutions because additional high-frequency content increases distractor-induced false positives without adding smoke-discriminative information, while solid-object accuracy rises monotonically over the same sweep.
falsifiable_prediction: Resolution sweeps on matched models will show a non-monotone accuracy curve for smoke datasets (with the peak shifting predictably with imaging distance) and monotone curves for solid-object controls; false-positive analysis will attribute the high-resolution decline to textured-distractor regions.
why_important: Deployment systems pay heavily for resolution (bandwidth, compute); a validated non-monotonicity would cut costs and improve accuracy simultaneously, and the spectral explanation refines the media prior of C-078.
why_possibly_novel: Resolution ablations exist for efficiency studies; a media-specific accuracy-optimal resolution with a spectral mechanism appears undocumented (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Resolution sweep across smoke and solid datasets with fixed-capacity models retrained per resolution, false-positive stratification by local frequency content.
main_risk: Model capacity and receptive field interact with resolution; the sweep must retrain per resolution with matched effective receptive fields or the curve reflects architecture mismatch, not information.
community_default_belief: Feed the highest resolution you can afford; information can only help.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Added pixels add distractor information and noise for targets that are spectrally band-limited; the optimum is set by the target's spectrum, not the sensor's capability.
fastest_falsification: Three-resolution sweep on one smoke dataset with one model.

one_line: Defocus blur dissociates media models' cue usage: smoke predictions should be blur-invariant while glass predictions collapse, and models violating this dissociation are using the wrong cues.
problem: There is no behavioral test that reveals which physical cues a media segmenter actually relies on; optical perturbations with known differential effects on cue classes could provide one, but none has been standardized.
core_hypothesis: Because smoke evidence is low-frequency and glass evidence is concentrated in high-frequency edges and speculars, controlled defocus should leave smoke segmentation nearly intact while degrading glass segmentation sharply; models deviating from this signature (smoke performance collapsing under blur) are relying on high-frequency background texture rather than medium appearance, predicting their failures on genuinely blurry deployment footage.
falsifiable_prediction: The blur-response curve of a well-grounded smoke model will be flat over moderate defocus while glass models degrade steeply; models with steep smoke blur-curves will disproportionately fail on naturally blurry footage (rain-smeared lenses, cheap optics), validating the curve as a cue-usage diagnostic.
why_important: A cheap optical behavioral test that predicts deployment robustness would let system integrators audit black-box models without internal access, and gives researchers a target invariance to train toward.
why_possibly_novel: Blur robustness is studied generically; using differential blur response as a cue-usage fingerprint across media classes with a deployment-prediction validation appears new (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Apply calibrated synthetic and real defocus to media benchmarks, measure per-model response curves, then test the correlation between smoke blur-sensitivity and error on curated naturally-blurry footage.
main_risk: Synthetic blur differs from real lens blur in ways models may detect; real defocused captures are needed for the validation arm, raising costs.
community_default_belief: Robustness to blur is a generic desideratum, uniform across classes, addressed by augmentation.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Blur is not noise for media tasks; it is a spectral filter whose effect is class-diagnostic because different materials carry evidence in different bands.
fastest_falsification: Blur-response curves for one smoke and one glass model over one dataset each.

one_line: Matting pretraining transfers to smoke better than segmentation pretraining, because the soft-boundary inductive bias matters more than semantic breadth.
problem: Transfer sources for media tasks are chosen by dataset size and semantic coverage (segmentation corpora), ignoring that the mechanical skill smoke requires (estimating fractional coverage) is what matting models practice; the comparison is absent from the literature.
core_hypothesis: At matched pretraining compute, models pretrained on alpha-matting objectives adapt to smoke segmentation faster and reach higher final quality (especially on boundary-band and thin-smoke metrics) than models pretrained on semantic segmentation, despite matting corpora being smaller and semantically narrower.
falsifiable_prediction: Few-shot and full fine-tuning comparisons will show matting-pretrained encoders dominating on boundary-band metrics and matching or exceeding on region metrics; the advantage will disappear when the downstream labels are heavily binarized, tying the effect to soft-boundary skill rather than generic features.
why_important: Pretraining choice is a zero-marginal-cost decision that the whole applied community makes by default; flipping the default for the media family would be an immediately actionable result.
why_possibly_novel: Task-affinity in transfer learning is studied broadly; the specific matting-beats-segmentation prediction for media, with the binarization control isolating the mechanism, appears untested (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Pretrain or obtain matched matting and segmentation checkpoints, fine-tune on smoke datasets at several shot counts, evaluate with band-decomposed metrics, run the binarized-label control.
main_risk: Public matting and segmentation checkpoints differ in architecture and data scale, making truly matched comparisons require expensive from-scratch pretraining.
community_default_belief: The largest, most diverse segmentation or general-vision pretraining is the best starting point for any dense task.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Transfer moves mechanisms as much as features; a smaller corpus that exercises the exact target mechanism (fractional assignment) may transfer the load-bearing skill that big corpora never induce.
fastest_falsification: Few-shot comparison at one shot count with the closest available public checkpoints.

one_line: Sensor noise, not architecture, is the binding constraint for thin-smoke segmentation: noise-matched training recovers more thin-smoke accuracy than any recent architectural improvement.
problem: Thin smoke lives near the sensor noise floor, yet training data comes from cleaner cameras than deployment hardware, and the community iterates on architecture while the noise mismatch goes unmodeled.
core_hypothesis: Injecting physically calibrated sensor noise (matched to deployment cameras) during training improves thin-smoke segmentation on noisy deployment footage by more than the cumulative gains of recent architecture generations measured on the same footage, because the models' thin-smoke features are currently fitted to noise statistics they will never see again.
falsifiable_prediction: On a fixed noisy-deployment test set, noise-matched retraining of an older architecture will outperform newer architectures trained conventionally; the gain will concentrate in the lowest-contrast smoke strata and vanish in high-contrast strata, confirming the noise-floor mechanism.
why_important: Would demonstrate that a free training-pipeline change dominates years of architectural work for the operationally critical thin-smoke regime, reordering the field's priorities toward sensor-aware training.
why_possibly_novel: Noise augmentation is common as generic robustness; the claim that calibrated noise matching dominates architectural progress for a specific physical regime appears unquantified (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Characterize deployment-camera noise, retrain matched old/new architectures with and without calibrated noise, evaluate on real noisy captures stratified by smoke contrast.
main_risk: The result depends on how badly current training data mismatches deployment noise; with modern phone footage in training sets the mismatch may already be small, nullifying the effect.
community_default_belief: Architectural and data-scale improvements are where thin-target robustness comes from; noise handling is a preprocessing detail.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Near the noise floor, the discriminative boundary is defined jointly by signal and noise statistics; training under the wrong noise learns a boundary that physically does not exist on the deployment camera.
fastest_falsification: Noise-matched retraining of one model, evaluated on one noisy test set.

one_line: Optimizing mask quality delays alarms: mask-IoU-optimal smoke models are systematically slower to first detection than 'worse' models, an objective-level conflict in early-warning systems.
problem: Early-warning pipelines are built from segmentation models selected by mask quality, assuming quality and timeliness align; the two objectives plausibly conflict because confident well-formed masks require developed plumes.
core_hypothesis: Across model pools and operating thresholds, there is a Pareto frontier between mask quality and detection latency on ignition timelines, and models at the IoU-optimal end sit far from the latency-optimal end: mask-quality selection costs meaningful detection time at fixed false-alarm budgets.
falsifiable_prediction: Joint measurement of IoU and latency on continuous ignition recordings will show a negative association among top models; threshold tuning alone will not close the gap, and latency-optimized training (loss weighting early faint smoke) will sacrifice IoU while improving time-to-alarm at equal false-alarm rate, tracing the frontier.
why_important: System integrators currently pick models by leaderboard mask metrics for a mission whose objective is latency; documenting the tradeoff would change procurement and evaluation practice in safety-critical deployments.
why_possibly_novel: Quality-latency tradeoffs are studied in streaming perception generally; establishing the conflict specifically between mask optimality and alarm latency for media appears new (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble ignition-timeline recordings, evaluate a model pool for both objectives at matched false-alarm rates, fit the frontier, run one latency-weighted training as the intervention arm.
main_risk: Latency differences may be driven mostly by detection-threshold policy layers rather than the segmentation models themselves; the analysis must isolate model-attributable latency.
community_default_belief: The best segmentation model is the best component for any downstream use, including alarms.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Mask metrics average over the visibility distribution while alarms depend on the earliest tail; optimizing the average provably permits sacrificing the tail, and training does what the loss permits.
fastest_falsification: IoU-vs-latency scatter of three models on a handful of timelines.

one_line: Untrained humans beat state-of-the-art models at incipient smoke detection via motion pop-out, indicating the missing computation is pre-attentive temporal salience, not recognition capacity.
problem: Model failures on early faint smoke are attributed to insufficient data or capacity, but human observers reportedly notice faint plumes effortlessly; a rigorous human-model comparison isolating the mechanism has not been run.
core_hypothesis: In matched-viewing conditions (same video, same monitors, forced-choice detection), novice humans outperform current models on incipient smoke primarily due to motion-based salience, since the human advantage shrinks or vanishes on single frames and on motion-nulled videos, localizing the models' deficit to temporal salience computation rather than smoke knowledge.
falsifiable_prediction: The human-model gap will be large on video, small on single frames, and near-zero on motion-scrambled video; a simple bio-inspired temporal-salience front end added to models will close a disproportionate share of the video gap, consistent with the mechanism diagnosis.
why_important: Identifies which computation to build rather than which dataset to scale, and provides a principled human baseline for early-detection benchmarks that currently lack one.
why_possibly_novel: Human-vs-model studies exist for object recognition; a mechanism-localizing design (frame vs motion vs scrambled) for incipient media detection appears absent (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Psychophysics-style forced-choice study with novices across the three viewing conditions on ignition timelines, matched model evaluation, then the salience front-end intervention.
main_risk: Human performance may rest on strategy and expectation effects hard to match to model evaluation protocols; task framing must be carefully equated.
community_default_belief: Models surpass humans on vigilance tasks; remaining gaps close with data and scale.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Vigilance superiority holds for sustained attention, not for extraction of weak coherent motion from noise, a computation biological early vision implements and current segmentation stacks demonstrably do not prioritize.
fastest_falsification: Small pilot (10 observers, 50 clips, three conditions) against two public models.

one_line: Clutter helps glass: transparent-object segmentation may be more accurate against complex backgrounds than clean ones, inverting the universal clutter-hurts assumption.
problem: Benchmarks and collection practices assume cluttered scenes are the hard case for all classes; for objects whose evidence is background distortion, clutter is signal, and the direction of the effect has never been isolated.
core_hypothesis: For fixed glass objects and lighting, segmentation accuracy increases with background texture density (up to saturation) because refraction and reflection evidence scales with background structure, while opaque-object accuracy decreases over the same manipulation; current models already exploit this even though their training assumed clutter is adversity.
falsifiable_prediction: A controlled background-complexity sweep (same objects, systematically varied backdrops) will show opposite-signed accuracy slopes for glass vs opaque controls across multiple public models; the glass slope will flatten only for flat low-distortion panes, consistent with the distortion mechanism.
why_important: Would invert data-collection guidance for transparency (seek textured contexts, not studio cleanliness), and sharpen theory about what evidence these models consume.
why_possibly_novel: Clutter effects are documented as harmful for detection; a demonstrated beneficial clutter regime tied to refractive evidence appears novel (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Tabletop sweep with parameterized backdrop textures, fixed camera and lighting, evaluation of several public models on both material classes.
main_risk: Clutter also increases reflection confusion (more content to mirror); the net slope may be non-monotone, requiring finer decomposition into transmission vs reflection evidence.
community_default_belief: Cluttered backgrounds degrade segmentation of every object class; clean captures are the easy case.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The generalization was induced from opaque objects, whose evidence is self-appearance; for see-through objects the background is the signal carrier, flipping the sign of the clutter effect.
fastest_falsification: Three-backdrop sweep (blank, moderate, dense texture) on a dozen glass objects with one model.

one_line: Physically correct but visually unrealistic synthetic smoke trains better models than photorealistic game-engine smoke: transfer is governed by image-formation correctness, not perceptual realism.
problem: Synthetic media pipelines optimize for human-judged realism (artistic tone mapping, stylized volumetrics), assuming realism drives transfer; the alternative axis, physical correctness of light transport, is confounded with realism and never independently manipulated.
core_hypothesis: In a factorial synthetic-data experiment crossing perceptual realism with physical correctness of compositing (correct Beer-Lambert attenuation and scattering vs artist-tuned blending), models trained on physically correct but unrealistic-looking data transfer to real smoke better than those trained on realistic-looking but physically incorrect data, because networks key on compositing statistics rather than aesthetic properties.
falsifiable_prediction: The physical-correctness factor will dominate the realism factor in real-world transfer performance; error analysis will show artist-blended-data models failing precisely where real attenuation deviates from their blending model (dense cores, backlit smoke).
why_important: The synthetic-data industry invests in realism; a validated correctness-over-realism ordering would redirect rendering budgets and clarify what the sim-to-real gap for media actually consists of.
why_possibly_novel: Domain randomization argues against realism for robustness; the specific decomposition into perceptual realism vs light-transport correctness for participating media appears untested (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build the 2x2 synthetic training sets from one scene corpus, train matched models, evaluate transfer on controlled real captures with density instrumentation.
main_risk: Fully crossing the factors is technically tricky (realism and correctness co-vary in most renderers); partial confounding would weaken attribution.
community_default_belief: The more photorealistic the synthetic data, the smaller the sim-to-real gap.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Networks consume pixel statistics generated by the compositing math, not the gestalt humans rate as realistic; if the math is wrong, realism is a decorated lie the model faithfully learns.
fastest_falsification: Two-cell version of the experiment (correct-unrealistic vs incorrect-realistic) with small models.

one_line: Boundary-precision label noise is a non-problem for media: aggressive random boundary jitter in training barely hurts smoke models, exposing that annotation-precision budgets are spent on a fiction.
problem: Dataset teams invest heavily in precise media boundaries assuming label precision converts to model quality; if models never learned boundary precision anyway (C-007, C-029), that investment is wasted, but the dose-response has never been measured.
core_hypothesis: Training smoke segmenters with deliberately jittered boundaries (random dilation/erosion of substantial magnitude) produces models statistically indistinguishable from precisely-labeled training on all region metrics and most boundary metrics, while the same jitter substantially degrades solid-object models, quantifying how little boundary information media models actually extract from labels.
falsifiable_prediction: The jitter dose-response curve for smoke will be flat up to large perturbation magnitudes and steep for solid controls; the flat region's extent will match the inter-annotator disagreement band, showing models were already learning only up to the ambiguity floor.
why_important: Directly converts to annotation-budget policy: money spent under the ambiguity floor is provably wasted and should move to coverage, scene diversity, or the negative-evidence labels of C-018.
why_possibly_novel: Label-noise robustness is studied generically; the media-specific flat-response prediction tied to the ambiguity floor, with budget implications, appears unmeasured (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Jitter-magnitude sweep on one smoke and one solid dataset with matched retraining, dose-response comparison against measured inter-annotator bands.
main_risk: Systematic (directional) jitter may behave differently from random jitter; the benign result may not license sloppy annotation whose errors are biased, requiring a biased-jitter control arm.
community_default_belief: Cleaner, tighter boundary annotation reliably improves segmentation models, so precision is worth paying for.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Model learning saturates at the label distribution's intrinsic ambiguity; beyond that floor, precision purchases digits of a number that has no next digit for media.
fastest_falsification: Two-point jitter experiment (none vs heavy) on one smoke dataset.

one_line: Models trained on composited synthetic smoke learn to detect compositing, not smoke: their real-world performance anticorrelates with their synthetic validation scores past a threshold.
problem: Synthetic smoke is typically composited over real backgrounds without consistent lighting interaction (no cast shadows, no local illumination changes); whether models exploit these compositing tells as shortcuts is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: Networks trained on naively composited data increasingly key on compositing artifacts (statistical seams, missing illumination coupling) as training progresses, so synthetic-validation accuracy keeps rising while real-transfer accuracy peaks early and declines, producing a measurable anticorrelation between the two curves in late training that lighting-coupled compositing eliminates.
falsifiable_prediction: Training-trajectory analysis will show real-transfer performance peaking well before synthetic validation saturates for naive compositing, with the divergence absent when composites include physically coupled lighting; artifact-detector probes will confirm growing reliance on seam statistics in the naive condition.
why_important: Early stopping and data-pipeline choices for the many groups using composited media data currently fly blind; the trajectory signature gives them a practical diagnostic, and the lighting-coupling result a fix.
why_possibly_novel: Compositing artifacts are a known risk in forgery detection; the training-dynamics anticorrelation signature as a shortcut-onset diagnostic for media appears new (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train models on naive vs lighting-coupled composites with dense checkpointing, evaluate every checkpoint on controlled real captures, plot the trajectory pair and probe for artifact reliance.
main_risk: The lighting-coupled condition is expensive to render at scale; a partial coupling implementation might blur the contrast between arms.
community_default_belief: Synthetic validation scores are a reasonable proxy for the value of synthetic training data; more synthetic accuracy means better transfer.
why_that_may_be_wrong: When the synthetic distribution contains a detectable generation fingerprint, the proxy inverts: optimizing it rewards fingerprint detection, the one skill guaranteed useless on real data.
fastest_falsification: Checkpoint-trajectory comparison on one naive-composite training run against a small real test set.

one_line: A fog-machine-metered capture protocol yields physically calibrated alpha labels at scale, and one thousand physically labeled images may outtrain one hundred thousand hand-labeled ones for density-aware tasks.
problem: Media datasets scale by hand-labeling found footage, inheriting every epistemological pathology in this shard; a capture protocol where ground truth is measured rather than judged has not been seriously costed or tested against the hand-labeled regime.
core_hypothesis: Background-subtraction against pre-release reference frames plus metered fog output provides per-pixel physically defined alpha labels with negligible marginal labeling cost, and models trained on modest volumes of such data outperform models trained on far larger hand-labeled corpora on density-sensitive evaluations (transmittance ranking, threshold-family prediction), while remaining competitive on conventional mask metrics.
falsifiable_prediction: The physically labeled training set will dominate hand-labeled training at equal model capacity on calibrated evaluations by large margins and trail only modestly on conventional benchmarks, with the conventional gap closing after light fine-tuning; per-label cost accounting will favor the protocol by an order of magnitude for alpha-quality supervision.
why_important: If measurement can replace judgment as the supervision source for media, the field escapes the annotator-threshold trap wholesale, and every idea in this shard requiring calibrated data gets its instrument.
why_possibly_novel: Controlled smoke captures exist for physics research; a costed, scaled protocol positioned as a training-data substitute with a head-to-head against hand labeling appears absent from the segmentation literature (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Execute the protocol across several dozen scenes and conditions, train matched models on physical vs hand labels, evaluate on both calibrated and conventional tests with cost accounting.
main_risk: Fog-machine aerosol differs from combustion smoke optically and dynamically; domain gap between calibration medium and target media could blunt the transfer claim and must be bounded with a small combustion-capture set.
community_default_belief: Scaling annotation of diverse real imagery is the only path to strong real-world media models.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The scaling path scales a corrupted supervision signal; a smaller uncorrupted signal can win whenever label fidelity, not image diversity, is the binding constraint, which the calibrated evaluations would reveal.
fastest_falsification: Pilot the protocol in five scenes, train a small model, test transmittance ranking against a hand-label-trained equivalent.

one_line: Cross-media transfer follows particle physics: generalization between fog, steam, smoke, and dust is predicted by scattering-regime similarity, giving a transfer matrix computable before any training.
problem: Practitioners guess which auxiliary media data helps a target medium; there is no predictive theory of cross-media transfer, though the media differ along physically characterized axes (particle size, albedo, density dynamics).
core_hypothesis: The empirical transfer matrix between media segmentation tasks (train on A, test on B) is well predicted by a physical similarity computed from scattering parameters and dynamic regime, so beneficial and harmful transfers are forecastable a priori, and apparent anomalies (steam helping smoke less than fog does, or vice versa) resolve under the physical metric rather than semantic intuition.
falsifiable_prediction: Measuring the full pairwise transfer matrix across the four media will show rank agreement with the physical-similarity matrix significantly above semantic or visual-similarity baselines; transfer failures will cluster where dynamic regimes differ despite appearance similarity (steam's condensation-evaporation vs smoke's dispersion).
why_important: Turns data-sourcing for any new medium (chemical releases, volcanic ash, sea spray) into a computation instead of an experiment, and validates a physics-grounded organizing principle for the whole territory.
why_possibly_novel: Task-transfer prediction exists via learned task embeddings; deriving the predictor from scattering physics for the media family appears unattempted (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble or capture labeled data per medium, train per-medium models, fill the transfer matrix, correlate against physical, semantic, and visual similarity predictors.
main_risk: Dataset-specific confounds (camera, scene types per medium) may dominate the matrix; captures should share protocol across media to isolate the medium factor.
community_default_belief: All white volumetric media are near-interchangeable as training data; pooling them is harmless and helpful.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Pooling across scattering regimes may teach regime-averaged features wrong for every regime, and the physical metric predicts exactly which pools poison which targets.
fastest_falsification: Two-by-two corner of the matrix (fog/smoke) under a shared capture protocol.

one_line: The real out-of-distribution axis for fire models is flame chemistry, not scene diversity: blue, invisible, and metal-fire flames define a failure family that scene-diverse datasets never touch.
problem: Fire dataset curation pursues scene diversity (forests, buildings, vehicles) while nearly all imaged flames share hydrocarbon-orange emission; combustion chemistry varies flame color, texture, and visibility radically, and model behavior across chemistry is uncharted.
core_hypothesis: Fire segmentation models fail on chemically atypical flames (alcohol blue, hydrogen near-invisible, metal-salt colored) at rates approaching total misses regardless of scene familiarity, and augmenting training with small amounts of chemistry-diverse data recovers most of the failure, demonstrating that the operative distribution axis was chemical, not environmental.
falsifiable_prediction: A chemistry-stratified test set (controlled burns of varied fuels) will show public models' recall collapsing on non-orange flames even in familiar scenes; scene-novel orange fires will fail far less, and chemistry-targeted fine-tuning with modest data will disproportionately restore performance.
why_important: Industrial fires (alcohol, hydrogen, metals) are precisely the high-consequence cases; safety systems validated on scene-diverse orange-fire benchmarks carry an invisible chemical blind spot.
why_possibly_novel: Fuel-type effects are known in combustion science; a chemistry-stratified audit of vision models and the chemistry-vs-scene axis comparison appear absent from the segmentation literature (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Controlled multi-fuel burn captures under safety supervision, evaluation of public models per fuel class, targeted fine-tuning arm with recovery measurement.
main_risk: Safe multi-fuel captures need specialist facilities; scale will be small, so claims must lean on effect size rather than breadth.
community_default_belief: Scene and environment diversity is the main generalization challenge for fire perception; flames themselves are visually homogeneous.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Flame appearance is emission spectroscopy made visible; fuel chemistry changes the object itself, a distribution shift categorically larger than background variation yet absent from every scraped dataset by sampling construction.
fastest_falsification: Run public models on a handful of alcohol-flame clips; near-total misses are immediate confirmation of the direction.

one_line: Scraped fire/smoke corpora are contaminated by viral-footage near-duplicates, inflating benchmark scores through train-test leakage that perceptual-hash auditing would expose.
problem: Dramatic fire footage is copied, re-encoded, and re-posted across the web at unusual rates compared to mundane imagery, so scraped datasets plausibly contain cross-split near-duplicates at levels unmeasured for this domain.
core_hypothesis: Near-duplicate contamination rates in scraped fire/smoke datasets substantially exceed those of general-purpose vision datasets due to viral propagation dynamics of disaster footage, and deduplicated re-evaluation measurably reduces reported scores and reorders methods, with memorization-prone (higher-capacity, longer-trained) models losing the most.
falsifiable_prediction: Perceptual-hash and embedding-based audits of commonly used scraped fire corpora will find cross-split near-duplicate rates well above general-dataset baselines; score drops after deduplication will correlate with model capacity, and at least some published-style ranking gaps will close or invert.
why_important: If the domain's benchmarks systematically overstate performance through leakage, deployment expectations and method comparisons are miscalibrated in a safety-relevant field; the audit protocol itself becomes a required hygiene step.
why_possibly_novel: Dataset duplication audits exist for large pretraining corpora; the domain-specific amplification hypothesis (viral disaster footage) and its benchmark consequences for media segmentation appear unexamined (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run multi-method near-duplicate detection within and across splits of scraped fire datasets, quantify contamination, re-evaluate public models on deduplicated splits.
main_risk: Near-duplicate detection thresholds are contestable (same fire, different camera is legitimate); results need sensitivity analysis across duplicate definitions.
community_default_belief: Standard random train/test splitting adequately isolates evaluation data in scraped domain datasets.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Random splitting assumes source independence; viral copying creates hidden many-to-one source structure that random splits distribute across both sides, guaranteeing leakage proportional to virality.
fastest_falsification: Perceptual-hash audit of one scraped corpus's train/test split.

one_line: Generated smoke is a new deployment class: segmenters respond identically to real and diffusion-generated smoke, opening a spoofing and false-alarm channel that real-vs-generated texture statistics could close.
problem: Synthetic smoke imagery now circulates widely (games, films, generated media shown on screens within scenes, doctored footage), yet media segmenters have no concept of generation provenance and their response to generated smoke is uncharacterized.
core_hypothesis: Current smoke segmenters respond to diffusion-generated and game-engine smoke indistinguishably from real smoke (full activation), even where generated smoke violates physical constraints (impossible illumination coupling, non-physical dynamics), meaning surveillance and monitoring pipelines can be triggered or spoofed by displayed or injected synthetic media; physically grounded consistency checks (temporal spectra, illumination coupling) can discriminate where appearance cannot.
falsifiable_prediction: Response-equivalence tests will show near-identical activation distributions on matched real vs generated smoke; physics-based consistency features will separate the classes substantially better than the segmenters' own confidence signals, providing a bolt-on discriminator.
why_important: Monitoring systems increasingly watch screens, projections, and potentially adversarial feeds; an uncharacterized equivalence between real and fabricated smoke is both a security hole and a growing false-alarm source as generated content saturates environments.
why_possibly_novel: Deepfake detection targets faces; the intersection of generated-content robustness with safety-critical media segmentation appears unexplored (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble matched real/generated smoke sets, measure segmenter response equivalence, implement physics-consistency discriminators, evaluate the bolt-on pipeline.
main_risk: Generation quality is a moving target; discriminating features validated today may decay, making the contribution the audit methodology more than any fixed feature set.
community_default_belief: Segmentation models need only handle the real visual world; generated content is a separate forensics problem.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The deployed visual world now contains generated content physically displayed within real scenes; the separation between segmentation and forensics is an assumption the environment has already violated.
fastest_falsification: Activation-equivalence measurement on one model with a small matched real/generated set.

one_line: Transparent-liquid dynamics are the missing hard case: static-biased glass datasets leave models helpless on pouring, splashing, and flowing water whose refractive geometry changes per frame.
problem: Transparent-object datasets consist almost entirely of static vessels and panes; transient liquid geometry (pours, streams, splashes) is refractive matter with per-frame shape, and no benchmark measures whether static-trained transparency competence extends to it.
core_hypothesis: Models trained on static transparency fail on dynamic liquids not gradually but categorically (treating streams as background disturbance or motion artifact), because their transparency evidence (stable rims, persistent speculars) is absent in transients; temporal integration of refraction cues, useless for static glass, becomes the dominant signal for liquids, so the static and dynamic problems require different mechanisms despite identical material.
falsifiable_prediction: A dynamic-liquid test set will show static-trained models near chance on streams and splashes while retaining vessel performance in the same frames; models augmented with short-window temporal refraction features will improve on transients specifically, and the improvement will not transfer back to static glass, confirming the mechanism split.
why_important: Kitchen and laboratory robotics, industrial dispensing, and spill detection all involve moving liquids; the field's static bias means its transparency competence claims silently exclude the useful cases.
why_possibly_novel: Liquid perception is studied for pouring control with depth sensors; an RGB segmentation benchmark and mechanism analysis for transient refractive matter appears missing (not verified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Capture and annotate a pouring/splashing test set with static vessels co-present, evaluate public models with within-frame stratification, prototype the temporal-refraction augmentation.
main_risk: Annotating fast transients is genuinely hard (motion blur, ambiguous droplet extents), risking label quality issues that confound the categorical-failure claim.
community_default_belief: Transparent-object segmentation progress on static benchmarks represents progress on transparency in general.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The static benchmarks sample the special case where transparency evidence is time-invariant; the general case inverts which cues exist, so static progress may measure a mechanism that generalizes nowhere beyond stillness.
fastest_falsification: Run public glass models on a dozen pouring clips; categorical stream misses alongside intact vessel masks is the immediate signal.
